Use **Ctrl+Z** to undo a weight change. ### Blending with `.blend()` [Section titled “Blending with .blend()”](#blending-with-blend) Use `.blend()` to mix the meaning of two or more prompts. 
```text
("portrait photo, 85mm lens", "oil painting, visible brushstrokes").blend(0.7, 0.3)
```
 Provide one weight for each prompt. Keeping the weights near a total of `1` makes the result easier to reason about, and quoting each prompt is safest, especially when they contain commas. ### Combining clauses with `.and()` [Section titled “Combining clauses with .and()”](#combining-clauses-with-and) Use `.and()` when you want separate prompt clauses encoded individually instead of as one long comma-separated sentence. 
```text
("red silk dress", "studio portrait", "soft rim light").and()
```
 This can behave differently from `red silk dress, studio portrait, soft rim light`. If a normal prompt keeps collapsing ideas together, `.and()` is worth testing. ### Literal parentheses [Section titled “Literal parentheses”](#literal-parentheses) Unescaped parentheses are treated as weighting syntax. To include actual parentheses in the text, escape them with backslashes: 
```text
colored pencil \(medium\)
A bear \(with razor-sharp teeth\) in a forest
```
 ## Advanced dynamic prompt syntax [Section titled “Advanced dynamic prompt syntax”](#advanced-dynamic-prompt-syntax) These additions to the [dynamic prompt](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/#dynamic-prompts) syntax give finer control over how variations are built. ### Choosing more than one option [Section titled “Choosing more than one option”](#choosing-more-than-one-option) Put a number and `$$` at the start of a group to pick several different options from it. They are joined with a comma: 
```text
portrait, {2$$rim light|fog|rain}
```
 gives prompts such as `portrait, rim light,fog` and `portrait, fog,rain`. To join them differently, put the separator between two `$$`: 
```text
portrait, {2$$ and $$rim light|fog|rain}
```
 gives prompts such as `portrait, rim light and fog`. A range picks a varying number of options: `{1-3$$rim light|fog|rain}` picks one, two or three. ### Weighting options [Section titled “Weighting options”](#weighting-options) In **Random sample** mode, you can make some options more likely than others by putting a weight and `::` in front of them: 
```text
a {0.7::red|0.2::green|0.1::blue} balloon
```
 makes red balloons most common. Weights are ignored in All combinations mode, where every option appears once. ### Variables [Section titled “Variables”](#variables) A variable gives a group a name, so you can define it once and use it in several places. `${name={...}}` defines it and `${name}` uses it: 
```text
${color={red|blue}} a ${color} hat with a ${color} scarf
```
 Each use varies on its own, like a group written out in full, so this gives all four combinations from `a red hat with a red scarf` to `a blue hat with a blue scarf`. Variables are most useful for long lists you would otherwise repeat; for lists you use in many prompts, a [wildcard](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/#wildcards) is more convenient. ### Comments [Section titled “Comments”](#comments) Everything after a `#` is treated as a comment and left out of the prompt. Avoid `#` in ordinary prompts, since the rest of the prompt after it is dropped.

# Diffusion

Taking the time to understand the diffusion process will help you to understand how to more effectively use InvokeAI. ## Image Space vs. Latent Space [Section titled “Image Space vs. Latent Space”](#image-space-vs-latent-space) There are two main ways Stable Diffusion works — with images, and latents. Image Space Represents images in pixel form that you look at. This is the final visual output you see. Latent Space Represents compressed inputs. It’s in latent space that Stable Diffusion processes images. ## Core Components [Section titled “Core Components”](#core-components) To fully understand the diffusion process, we need to understand a few more terms: **U-Net**, **CLIP**, and **conditioning**. U-Net A model trained on a large number of latent images with known amounts of random noise added. The U-Net can be given a slightly noisy image and it will predict the pattern of noise needed to subtract from the image in order to recover the original. CLIP & Conditioning **CLIP** is a model that tokenizes and encodes text into **conditioning**. This conditioning guides the model during the denoising steps to produce a new image. The U-Net and CLIP work together during the image generation process at each denoising step. The U-Net removes noise so that the result is similar to images in its training set, while CLIP guides the U-Net towards creating images that are most similar to your prompt. ## The Generation Process [Section titled “The Generation Process”](#the-generation-process) * Text-to-Image When you generate an image using text-to-image, multiple steps occur in latent space: 1. **Noise Generation:** Random noise is generated at the chosen height and width. The noise’s characteristics are dictated by the seed. This noise tensor is passed into latent space. We’ll call this *noise A*. 2. **Noise Prediction:** Using a model’s U-Net, a noise predictor examines *noise A* and the words tokenized by CLIP from your prompt (conditioning). It generates its own noise tensor to predict what the final image might look like in latent space. We’ll call this *noise B*. 3. **Subtraction:** *Noise B* is subtracted from *noise A* in an attempt to create a latent image consistent with the prompt. This step is repeated for the number of sampler steps chosen. 4. **Decoding:** The VAE decodes the final latent image from latent space into image space. * Image-to-Image Image-to-image is a similar process, with only the first step being different: 1. **Encoding & Adding Noise:** The input image is encoded from image space into latent space by the VAE. Noise is then added to the input latent image. * **Denoising Strength** dictates how many noise steps are added, and the amount of noise added at each step. * A strength of `0` means there are 0 steps and no noise added, resulting in an unchanged image. * A strength of `1` results in the image being completely replaced with noise and a full set of denoising steps are performed. 2. **Noise Prediction:** Using a model’s U-Net, a noise predictor examines the noisy latent image and the conditioning from your prompt. It generates its own noise tensor to predict the final image. 3. **Subtraction:** The predicted noise is subtracted from the current noise in an attempt to create a latent image consistent with the prompt. This step is repeated for the remaining sampler steps. 4. **Decoding:** The VAE decodes the final latent image from latent space into image space. ## Summary [Section titled “Summary”](#summary) Putting it all together * A **Model** provides the CLIP prompt tokenizer, the VAE, and a U-Net (where noise prediction occurs given a prompt and initial noise tensor). * A **Noise Scheduler** (e.g. `DPM++ 2M Karras`) schedules the subtraction of noise from the latent image across the sampler steps chosen. Less noise is usually subtracted at higher sampler steps.

# HiDiffusion

# HiDiffusion [Section titled “HiDiffusion”](#hidiffusion) HiDiffusion is an optional denoising enhancement that can improve detail and structure at higher resolutions for SD 1.5, SD 2.1, and SDXL. It modifies the UNet during denoising and is most noticeable at 1536px and above. The vendored implementation includes module-key definitions for SD 1.5 and SDXL. SD 2.1 intentionally reuses the SD 1.5 module-key mapping. Learn more: <https://github.com/megvii-research/HiDiffusion> ## Where to find the switches [Section titled “Where to find the switches”](#where-to-find-the-switches) 1. Open the **Canvas** tab. 2. Expand **Advanced Settings**. 3. In the **Advanced** grid, enable **HiDiffusion** and optionally adjust the two sub‑toggles and ratios: * **HiDiffusion: RAU‑Net** * **HiDiffusion: Window Attention** * **HiDiffusion: T1 Ratio** * **HiDiffusion: T2 Ratio** ## What the switches do [Section titled “What the switches do”](#what-the-switches-do) * **HiDiffusion**: Enables the HiDiffusion patch for denoising. Use this for high‑resolution generations; the effect is subtle at lower sizes. * **HiDiffusion: RAU‑Net**: Enables RAU‑Net blocks. This typically improves structure and mid‑frequency detail, especially at larger resolutions. * **HiDiffusion: Window Attention**: Enables windowed attention blocks. This can boost local texture/detail, but may slightly affect global coherence in some prompts. * **HiDiffusion: T1 Ratio**: Controls when HiDiffusion switches into its mid‑stage behavior. Lower values switch earlier; higher values preserve global structure longer. * **HiDiffusion: T2 Ratio**: Controls when HiDiffusion switches into its late‑stage behavior. Higher values keep window attention active longer and can sharpen local detail. ## Tips [Section titled “Tips”](#tips) * Try **1536–2048 px** for the clearest benefits (SDXL). * If results look worse, disable **Window Attention** first, then RAU‑Net. * Effects vary by scheduler and model; compare with the same seed for a fair test.

# PiD Super-Resolution Decode

**PiD** (Pixel Diffusion Decoder) is an alternative way to turn a model’s latents into an image. Instead of the usual VAE decode, it runs a short pixel-space diffusion that produces a **4× super-resolved** result in a single, few-step pass — so a 512×512 generation comes out as a detailed 2048×2048 image. Because it decodes in pixel space and is conditioned on your prompt, PiD often recovers finer texture and edge detail than a plain VAE decode followed by an upscaler. ## Supported models [Section titled “Supported models”](#supported-models) PiD works with these base models: | Base model | PiD decoder to install | | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | FLUX.1 | PiD Decoder FLUX | | FLUX.2 Klein (4B / 9B) | PiD Decoder FLUX.2 | | Stable Diffusion 3 | PiD Decoder SD3 | | SDXL | PiD Decoder SDXL | | Z-Image / Z-Image Turbo | **PiD Decoder FLUX** (Z-Image shares FLUX.1’s VAE) | | Qwen-Image | PiD Decoder Qwen-Image | ## What you need to install [Section titled “What you need to install”](#what-you-need-to-install) PiD needs two extra models, both available in **Model Manager → Starter Models**: 1. A **PiD Decoder** for your base model (e.g. *PiD Decoder FLUX (2K)*). Some bases offer a *2K* and a *2K-to-4K* preset; SDXL and Qwen-Image ship only the *2K-to-4K* preset. 2. The **Gemma 2 2B (PiD caption encoder)** — PiD uses it to condition the decode on your prompt. It installs automatically as a dependency of any PiD decoder, and is shared across all of them. A first-generation PiD decoder download is roughly 5 GB, a PiD 1.5 decoder download roughly 2.8 GB (1.6 GB for its int8 build), and the shared Gemma-2 encoder is roughly 5 GB. Once loaded, a decoder runs in full precision and takes about 5.6 GB in either generation; the PiD 1.5 int8 build keeps its transformer layers in int8 and takes about 2 GB. The Gemma-2 caption encoder can also be a single-file **GGUF** (e.g. `gemma-2-2b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf`) that you install manually: InvokeAI loads it natively, keeping the large projection weights quantized instead of expanding them in memory, which cuts the encoder’s footprint noticeably. Only Gemma-2-**2b** GGUFs are accepted — PiD’s caption projection is fixed to their 2304-dim hidden state. ## Enabling PiD [Section titled “Enabling PiD”](#enabling-pid) Open the **Generation** settings for a supported model and expand the advanced options. You’ll find a **PiD Decode** control with three modes: * Off Standard VAE decode. No PiD models required. * Fit Generate at the requested size, decode 4× with PiD, then downscale the result back to the requested size. This is the safe default and works everywhere — the output matches your bounding box exactly, so it composites cleanly on the Canvas. * Native Treat the requested dimensions as the **4× target**: the image is generated at target ÷ 4 and PiD’s full 4× output is used directly (no downscale), preserving all of the added detail. Great when you want a large, highly-detailed result. When PiD mode is not *Off*, pick your **PiD Decoder** and **Gemma-2 Encoder** below the mode selector. The **PiD Steps** control (default 4) sets how many decode steps run — the released checkpoints are trained for 4. PiD is available in both the **Generate** tab (text-to-image) and on the **Canvas** (image-to-image), in both Fit and Native modes. ## Running PiD on an existing image [Section titled “Running PiD on an existing image”](#running-pid-on-an-existing-image) Everything above describes PiD as a *decode* step: it needs the latent the model just produced, so it only exists inside a generation. If you want to push an image you already have through PiD, the Workflow editor has a separate **PiD Upscale (4x)** node. It encodes your image with the FLUX VAE and hands the resulting latent to the PiD decoder, giving a 4× result in one pass — the PiD analogue of an ESRGAN / SUPIR upscale. Connect a FLUX VAE, a **FLUX** PiD decoder and the Gemma-2 encoder, and optionally give it a caption describing the image (the decoder is caption-conditioned; an empty caption is the cheapest option but usually the weaker result). Caution This node is a **prototype** and FLUX-only in both directions: it requires the FLUX.1 VAE (which Z-Image also uses; a VAE of another family is rejected) and a FLUX PiD decoder. Since the input is a plain image rather than the generating model’s own latent, results are less faithful than PiD used as a decode. ## Tips & limitations [Section titled “Tips & limitations”](#tips--limitations) On GPUs with limited VRAM, enable the experimental PiD memory optimizations in `invokeai.yaml`, then restart InvokeAI: 
```yaml
pid_memory_optimization: true
```
 This setting applies to every supported PiD decoder. It reduces peak activation and sampler memory by processing parts of the pixel pathway in chunks and by running the sampler’s intermediates in float32 instead of float64 — measured on an RTX 4090, a 2048px decode takes about 2.7–3.4 GB of VRAM on top of the decoder instead of 5.5–6.1 GB, and a 4096px decode about 11–14 GB, which fits on a 24 GB card only with this setting enabled. Decoding speed is roughly unchanged. It is disabled by default because it **changes the decoded image**. The combined optimized path is not guaranteed to be bit-exact with the default path: chunking can change GPU kernel and reduction choices, while the float32 sampler math differs from the default float64 path. The few-step sampler amplifies that into a small but real difference (\~43 dB PSNR — visually indistinguishable, numerically not identical). A seed that reproduced an image with the setting off will not reproduce it exactly with the setting on, and because this is a server-wide `invokeai.yaml` option it is not recorded in image metadata — each decode logs that it ran optimized instead. * **Turn off “Scale Before Processing”** on the Canvas when using PiD — PiD already decodes at 4×, so pre-scaling would inflate the work and is blocked. * **Inpaint / Outpaint** are not supported with PiD yet; use text-to-image or image-to-image. * **SDXL Refiner** cannot be combined with PiD — disable one of them. * PiD’s memory use scales with the *output* resolution. A 2048px output needs only a little more headroom than a normal decode, but Native mode at large target sizes (e.g. a 4096px result) is significantly heavier. * Turbo variants (e.g. Z-Image Turbo) work as usual — the low step count / no-CFG only affects generation; PiD’s own step count is separate. Caution The PiD decoder *code* is Apache-2.0, but NVIDIA releases the pretrained *weights* under a non-commercial / research license. Keep that in mind if you redistribute the checkpoints.

# Generate Panel Reference

> Every section of the Generate panel in detail — size, render settings, negative prompts, advanced options, resetting to defaults, concepts, reference images and the prompt tools.

This page describes each section of the **Generate** panel in detail. For a first walkthrough — choosing a model, generating a first image, and sending results to the Gallery or the Canvas — see [Generating and modifying still images](/users-guide/image-generation/introduction/). ## Setting the image size [Section titled “Setting the image size”](#setting-the-image-size) The **Size** section sets the width and height of the image. * **Width** and **Height** can be set by dragging, by typing a value, or by dragging the corner of the small size preview. Sizes run from 64 to 4096 pixels and snap to a multiple the model requires, usually 8, 16 or 32. * **Aspect ratio** offers common shapes: 21:9, 16:9, 3:2, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16 and 9:21, or **Free**. Choosing a ratio locks it, so changing the width changes the height to match. The lock button between the two fields locks or unlocks the current ratio. * **Swap width and height** turns a landscape image into a portrait one and back. * Each model has an optimal image area, typically about one megapixel for newer models and less for SD 1.5. The line under the fields shows the image’s size in megapixels, marks the recommended size, and estimates the run time from your recent runs. **Set optimal size** resizes the image to the model’s optimal area at the current aspect ratio. Models produce their best results near their optimal size. Much larger images can show repeated subjects or distorted anatomy. To make a large image, generate at the optimal size and then upscale. ## Render settings [Section titled “Render settings”](#render-settings) The **Render** section controls how the image is generated. Each slider has a mark at the model’s recommended value. To reset a single field, double-click it or right-click it and choose **Reset to model default**. ### Steps [Section titled “Steps”](#steps) **Steps** is the number of denoising passes the model makes. More steps add detail and refine the image, up to a point where further steps change little and only take longer. Distilled “Turbo” and “Lightning” models are designed for a handful of steps (often 4 to 9), while standard models usually need 25 to 50. The model default is a good place to start. ### CFG and Guidance [Section titled “CFG and Guidance”](#cfg-and-guidance) **CFG** (classifier-free guidance) sets how strictly the model follows your prompt. Higher values follow the prompt more literally but can look harsh or oversaturated; lower values are looser and more natural. Typical values are 3 to 7 for most models, and 1 for distilled models, which are trained to work without CFG. Some models, including FLUX, show **Guidance** instead: a value built into the model that plays the same role, typically around 3.5. The model’s page under Local Models gives recommended values. ### Scheduler [Section titled “Scheduler”](#scheduler) The **Scheduler** is the algorithm that decides how much noise to remove at each step. Schedulers differ in speed, in how many steps they need, and in the character of the result. Euler, the DPM++ family and UniPC are good general-purpose choices; LCM is only for LCM and similar distilled models. The list of schedulers depends on the model, and some models use a fixed schedule and do not show this field. **Use model default scheduler** switches back to the model’s own choice. ### Seed [Section titled “Seed”](#seed) The **Seed** sets the starting noise for the image. The same model, prompt, seed and settings reproduce the same image, which lets you change one setting at a time and compare the results. * **New seed** picks a random seed. * **Seed mode** sets how seeds are chosen: **Random** picks a fresh starting seed each time you press Invoke, **Fixed** reuses the seed in the field, and **Increment** and **Decrement** use successive seeds, counting up or down by one. A line under the field shows the seeds the next batch will use. * **Recent seeds** shows thumbnails of recent images. Click one to reuse its seed; the mode switches to Fixed. ### Negative prompt [Section titled “Negative prompt”](#negative-prompt) A negative prompt lists what you do *not* want in the image, such as *blurry, watermark, extra fingers*. Models that support one show a **+ Negative prompt…** button under the prompt; click it to open the box, and click **Turn off negative prompt** to hide it again without losing the text. Not every model uses a negative prompt. SD 1.5, SDXL, SD 3.5 and CogView4 always use it. Several newer models, including Z-Image, Qwen Image and Krea-2, use it only when CFG is above 1, and the box says so. FLUX.1, FLUX.2 and Ideogram 4 do not use a negative prompt, and the box is not shown for them. ### Advanced settings [Section titled “Advanced settings”](#advanced-settings) The **Advanced** section appears for models with extra options, and its header counts the settings you have changed. Depending on the model it can include: * **VAE** and **VAE precision** — for SD 1.5 and SDXL, choose a different VAE or decode at FP32 precision. Other families set their VAE in the Components section. * **CLIP skip** and **CFG rescale** — SD 1.5 and SD 2.x only. * **HiDiffusion** — improves structure at large sizes for SD 1.5 and SDXL; see [HiDiffusion](/users-guide/image-generation/advanced-topics/hidiffusion/). * **Color compensation** — SDXL only. * **PiD Decode** — decodes the image at up to four times its size; see [PiD Super-Resolution Decode](/users-guide/image-generation/advanced-topics/pid-decode/). * **Seamless tiling** — makes the image tile along the X axis, the Y axis, or both. ### Resetting to defaults [Section titled “Resetting to defaults”](#resetting-to-defaults) Each model has recommended settings, which you can change in the Model Manager. **Reset all to model defaults**, the ↺ button in the Generate panel’s title bar, applies them: size, steps, CFG or guidance, scheduler and VAE settings. Your prompts are left alone. The button is disabled when your settings already match the defaults. To return to the settings of an earlier image instead, right-click it in the Gallery or Preview and open **Recall Metadata**. **Recall All** restores its model, concepts, prompts, seed, size and render settings; **Remix Image** does the same but keeps a new seed; and **Use Prompt**, **Use Seed** and **Use Size** recall one thing at a time. Recalled concepts replace the ones in the panel at the weights the image used; any that are not installed or do not fit the model are listed in a notice. If the image’s model is not installed, or the image was saved from the canvas, your current concepts are kept. To keep a combination of settings for later, use **Presets** in the panel’s title bar to save the current settings under a name and apply them again. ## Adding concepts [Section titled “Adding concepts”](#adding-concepts) Concepts, also called LoRAs, are small add-on models that teach the main model a style, a character, an object or a look. They are added in the **Guidance** section. 1. Click **Add concept** and choose a LoRA. The list only shows LoRAs made for the selected model’s family. 2. Adjust its **Weight**, which sets how strongly it acts. The default is the LoRA’s own recommended weight, or 0.75. Values between 0.5 and 1 are typical; higher values can overpower the image, and negative values push the image away from the concept. 3. Add any trigger words the LoRA needs to your prompt. They are shown under the LoRA’s name, and the **+** button in the prompt toolbar inserts them for you (see [Prompt Triggers](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/#prompt-triggers)). You can add as many concepts as you like and combine them. Use the switch on each row to turn a concept off without removing it, and the trash button to remove it. If you change to a model from a different family, its concepts are marked **Incompatible** or removed. SD3, CogView4, ERNIE Image, Ideogram 4 and external API models don’t support concepts, so with one of them selected the section says so instead of offering LoRAs. ## Adding reference images [Section titled “Adding reference images”](#adding-reference-images) A reference image guides the new image by example rather than by words: its style, its composition, a person or an object in it. Reference images are added at the top of the **Guidance** section, and only appear for models that support them. To add one, click **Add reference image** and pick images from the Gallery or upload new ones, or drag images from the Gallery onto the section. You can also right-click any image and choose **Use as Reference Image**. Most models accept up to five. The order of the references matters to some models; use the arrow buttons on each card to reorder them. Hovering over a reference’s thumbnail offers **Crop**, to use only part of the image, and **Use size**, to set the generation’s size to match the reference. The switch on each card turns a reference off without removing it. What a reference does, and what options it has, depends on the model family: | Model family | How references work | Options | | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **SD 1.5, SDXL** | An IP-Adapter model carries the reference’s look into the image. | **Mode**: **Style**, **Composition** or **Both**. **Weight**. Under **Advanced**: the IP-Adapter model, a **Style variant** and the **Active steps** range. | | **FLUX.1** | An IP-Adapter, or a **FLUX Redux** model, which transfers the reference’s content. | IP-Adapter options as above, or **Image influence** (Lowest to Highest) for Redux. | | **FLUX.1 Kontext** | Kontext edits or recombines the reference images according to your prompt. | None beyond the model. | | **FLUX.2, Qwen Image Edit** | The model reads the references directly and uses them as your prompt instructs, for example *put the jacket from the first image on the person in the second*. | None. | Reference images require an extra model for SD 1.5, SDXL and FLUX.1 (an IP-Adapter or FLUX Redux model). These are available as starter models in the Model Manager, and an installed IP-Adapter is selected automatically. ## Prompt tools [Section titled “Prompt tools”](#prompt-tools) The toolbar above the prompt box holds tools that help you write prompts. From left to right: **Templates**, **Dynamic**, **Add prompt trigger**, **Expand prompt**, **Image to prompt** and **Prompt history**. ### Prompt enhancement [Section titled “Prompt enhancement”](#prompt-enhancement) **Expand prompt** turns a short prompt into a detailed description using a local language model. Write a few words, open the tool, pick a Text LLM and a **System prompt** (the instructions that tell the language model how to rewrite), and click **Expand**. The expanded text replaces your prompt, and you can edit it before pressing Invoke. Several system prompts ship with InvokeAI, some tuned for particular model families, and you can write your own. You need a Text LLM model installed; if there is none, the tool offers to open the Model Manager. See [Prompt Tools](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/#expand-prompt) for suitable models and for managing system prompts. ### Image to prompt [Section titled “Image to prompt”](#image-to-prompt) **Image to prompt** writes a prompt that describes an existing image, using a vision-language model (LLaVA OneVision). Select an image in the Gallery or Preview, or drag one onto the prompt box, then open the tool, choose the model and click **Generate Prompt**. The description replaces your prompt. This is useful for recreating an image you like in another model, or for starting from a close description and editing it. See [Prompt Tools](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/#image-to-prompt). ### Prompt history [Section titled “Prompt history”](#prompt-history) Every prompt you submit with Invoke is kept in the project’s **Prompt history**, along with its negative prompt, up to the last 100. Open it from the clock button to search your earlier prompts, click **Use prompt** to bring one back, or delete entries you no longer need. **Clear** empties the history at once, without asking. To step through the history without opening it, press **Alt+Up** and **Alt+Down** while the prompt box has focus. Stepping past the newest entry brings back what you were typing. The history belongs to the project and is shared by the Generate, Video and Upscale panels. ## More prompting features [Section titled “More prompting features”](#more-prompting-features) These features change what the prompt says or how the model reads it. Prompt triggers are described on the [Prompt Tools](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/) page, and the others in the [Prompting Guide](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/). | Feature | What it does | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **[Prompt templates](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/#prompt-templates)** | Wrap your prompt in a reusable style, such as a photographic or concept-art look, without retyping it. Includes 18 built-in templates, and you can create, import and export your own. | | **[Dynamic prompts](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/#dynamic-prompts)** | Write alternatives such as `a {red\|green\|blue} car` to generate one image per combination, or a random sample of them. Wildcards let you reuse named lists of values. | | **[Attention weighting](/users-guide/image-generation/advanced-prompt-syntax/#attention-weighting)** | Make parts of the prompt count for more or less, for example `(red car)++` or `(red car)1.3`, and blend or combine prompts. Select text and press **Ctrl+Up** or **Ctrl+Down** to adjust its weight. Applies to SD 1.5, SD 2.x and SDXL. | | **[Prompt triggers](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/#prompt-triggers)** | Insert the trigger phrases of your model and concepts, compatible embeddings and wildcards from a searchable menu. |

# Concepts and Terms

> A short glossary of the ideas and terms you meet when generating images — models, prompts, steps, CFG, schedulers, seeds, latents, LoRAs, ControlNets and more — with links to the guides that cover them.

New to AI image generation? This page explains the terms you will meet in InvokeAI, in plain language, and points to the guides that cover each one in depth. To start generating straight away, see [Generating and modifying still images](/users-guide/image-generation/introduction/). ## How an image is made [Section titled “How an image is made”](#how-an-image-is-made) Most image models in InvokeAI are **diffusion models**. A diffusion model starts from random noise and, over a series of **steps**, gradually removes the noise until an image remains, steered at every step by your prompt. The work happens on a compressed version of the image, the **latents**, which is decoded into pixels at the end. The [Diffusion overview](/users-guide/image-generation/advanced-topics/diffusion/) explains the process in more detail. ## Glossary [Section titled “Glossary”](#glossary) **Model.** The trained network that generates images. Models come in families, such as SD 1.5, SDXL, FLUX and Z-Image, which differ in size, speed, quality and the add-ons they accept. See [Managing media generation models](/users-guide/models/introduction/). **Prompt.** The text that describes the image you want. Many models also accept a **negative prompt** listing what you do not want. See the [Prompting Guide](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/). **Steps.** How many denoising passes the model makes. More steps refine detail up to a point, after which they change little. Standard models typically use 25 to 50 steps; distilled “Turbo” and “Lightning” models are designed for 4 to 10. **CFG (classifier-free guidance) or Guidance.** How strictly the model follows the prompt. Higher values follow it more literally; too high looks harsh or oversaturated. Distilled models usually run at a CFG of 1. **Scheduler.** The method that decides how much noise to remove at each step. Different schedulers trade speed, step count and character of the result. Some model families use a fixed schedule. **Seed.** The number that sets the starting noise. The same model, prompt, seed and settings reproduce the same image, which makes it easy to see what a single change does. **Latents.** The compressed form of an image that diffusion models work on. The **VAE** (variational autoencoder) converts between latents and pixels. **Text encoder.** The part of a model that turns the prompt into numbers the model understands. Older models use CLIP; newer ones use large language models, which understand long, detailed prompts. **Image to image.** Generating from an existing image instead of from pure noise. **Denoising strength** sets how much of the original is kept. **Inpainting and outpainting.** Regenerating part of an image (inpainting) or extending it beyond its edges (outpainting), done on the [Canvas](/users-guide/canvas/introduction/). **LoRA (concept).** A small add-on model that teaches the main model a style, character or object. Added in the Generate panel’s Guidance section. See [Adding concepts](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#adding-concepts). **Embedding (textual inversion).** A trained word that stands for a style or concept, inserted into the prompt as `<name>`. **Trigger phrase.** A word or phrase a LoRA or model needs in the prompt to produce its effect. See [Prompt Tools](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/#prompt-triggers). **ControlNet and control layers.** Add-on models that guide the composition with an image such as edges, depth or a pose. See [Control layers](/users-guide/canvas/introduction/#control-layers). **Reference image (IP-Adapter, Redux).** An image that guides the result by example, for its style, composition or content. See [Adding reference images](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#adding-reference-images). **Distilled model.** A model trained to produce good results in very few steps, usually at a CFG of 1, trading some flexibility for speed. Often named *Turbo*, *Lightning* or *Schnell*. **Quantized model.** A model stored at reduced precision, such as GGUF, fp8, int8 or nf4, to save memory and disk space at a small cost in quality. See [Checkpoints vs Diffusers formats](/users-guide/models/model-families/#checkpoints-vs-diffusers-formats). **Workflow.** A graph of processing steps that you build yourself in the workflow editor. See [Automating with Workflows](/users-guide/workflows/introduction/). ## Learn more [Section titled “Learn more”](#learn-more) * [Generating and modifying still images](/users-guide/image-generation/introduction/) — the Generate panel, step by step. * [Prompting Guide](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/) — writing prompts that work, and the tools that extend them. * [Parameter Selection Guide](/users-guide/image-generation/parameters/) — choosing steps, CFG, schedulers and seeds. * [This presentation](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1IO78i8oEXFTZ5peuHHYkVF-Y3e2M6iM5tCnc-YBfcCM/edit?usp=sharing) by one of the maintainers (@lstein) introduces the ideas behind AI image generation.

# Intermediates

> Reclaim disk space by deleting the temporary images and videos generation leaves behind, per project and per account.

Generation produces intermediate images and videos: canvas composites, filter previews, staging candidates and other temporary files that were never saved to the gallery. The **Intermediates** section of Settings lists them per project, shows how much space deleting them would reclaim, and deletes them safely. It is also reachable from a project’s actions menu, from the Users page (administrators) and from **Data & workspace**. ## What the page shows [Section titled “What the page shows”](#what-the-page-shows) Each row is one of your projects, or **Unassigned** for intermediates without a known project. Deleted projects’ leftovers appear under Unassigned. A row shows the project’s cover, its **Used** count (intermediates a cleanup keeps) and its **Unused** count (intermediates nothing needs any more), with the measured reclaimable size underneath. Sizes are measured in the background after upgrading; the section says so while measurement is still running and never counts an unmeasured file as empty. Select rows, or **Select all**, and press **Delete**. Select all covers every project the current search matches, including projects on other pages; untick a row to leave it out (up to 1,000 rows). A selection that matches more than 10,000 rows is refused; narrow the search. The confirmation explains why kept items are kept: referenced by a saved document, used by queued or running work, or created recently. Administrators start on their own account. **Show everyone** expands the view to every account; they can search accounts as well as project names and can open one account from the Users page. Opening the section from a project action shows that project directly, even when it is outside the first results page. ## Safe and force deletion [Section titled “Safe and force deletion”](#safe-and-force-deletion) A normal delete removes only safe items. It always keeps: * anything a pending, waiting or running job produced or uses as an input, including cached images and videos reused from an earlier job and completed child-workflow media until the root workflow finishes; * anything created in the last 30 minutes, so an upload the browser is about to reference or enqueue is never collected, and cached media for 30 minutes after the job that reused it ends; * anything the open webv2 editor still references, including unsaved edits and available undo history; the browser refreshes this temporary hold while it is open; * anything a saved document still names: a project or library workflow (canvas staging candidates, cropped reference images), the legacy editor’s saved canvas and reference images, or a project set aside for repair when project boards were introduced; * anything that is no longer an intermediate. The advanced option in the confirmation, **also delete items that saved projects or workflows still reference**, turns it into a force delete. The confirmation lists the documents it would break (the first 200, with a count of any others); those projects will show missing images and undo may no longer restore them. Confirming acknowledges exactly those documents: a document saved after the check keeps its media, while a document on the list may lose more of its references if it names further items while the deletion runs. A force delete never touches active, browser-held or recent work and cannot be undone; it asks for an acknowledgement and for the word `DELETE` to be typed. A regular user’s force delete also keeps anything another account’s document names, such as a shared workflow. The same applies when an administrator loses administrator rights while their force delete runs. A force delete that would break more than 10,000 documents is refused; narrow the selection. Every confirmation is based on a fresh server check that fixes the moment recency is judged at. Files created after the check are never included, and every batch re-checks its targets at the moment of deletion: an intermediate that was promoted, referenced or picked up by a job in the meantime is kept. Items that became unused after the check are collected too, so the deleted count can exceed the estimate. An open editor refreshes its browser hold every five minutes and when the tab becomes visible again. It releases names removed from the current projects and undo history, and releases the whole hold when the tab closes or you sign out. If the tab crashes instead, the hold expires 15 minutes after its last refresh. Each account holds media for at most eight open editors (tabs) at once; past that, the editor refreshed longest ago stops protecting its media until its next refresh. A single editor holds up to 50,000 images and 50,000 videos. Reopen an unsaved browser-only draft before deleting old intermediates. ## Progress and results [Section titled “Progress and results”](#progress-and-results) Cleanup runs on the server, so you can navigate away while it works. The page reports deleted, kept and failed items separately, along with files whose records are gone but whose bytes could not be removed yet; those are purged on the next server start and are not counted as reclaimed. Reloading the page, or opening the section with no deletion shown, picks up a deletion that is still running. When a deletion stops early or leaves failed items, **Delete again** repeats the same request, in the same mode; the check runs afresh, so it picks up exactly what remains. Running deletions live in the server’s memory. If the server restarts while one runs, the section still showing it reports that its status is no longer known; after a reload the interrupted run is simply gone. Either way, refresh the list and delete again if anything remains. The server keeps each account’s last few finished deletions until it restarts. The server accepts one running deletion per account and at most eight at a time. Wait for one to finish before confirming another delete if a limit is reached. Cleanup is refused while [image storage maintenance](/users-guide/gallery/image-storage-maintenance/) is active. ## Permissions [Section titled “Permissions”](#permissions) | Action | Regular user | Administrator | | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | | Delete a project’s intermediates | Own projects | Any project | | Delete an account’s intermediates | Own account | Any account | | Delete everyone’s intermediates | No | Yes | | Force delete referenced intermediates | Own files that only your own documents name | Any authorized scope | ## Legacy endpoint [Section titled “Legacy endpoint”](#legacy-endpoint) The older `DELETE /api/v1/images/intermediates` route remains available to administrators. It applies the same safety policy as a normal delete, so it keeps referenced, active and recent images and returns the number of images it deleted. It does not touch videos. `GET /api/v1/images/intermediates` counts exactly the images that route would delete, so the legacy button settles at zero after it runs. ## Limitations [Section titled “Limitations”](#limitations) * Canvas uploads made before the server accepted the project they belong to are stored without a project and are never re-associated with it. They are still protected by saved references and browser holds, but they appear under **Unassigned**.

# Generating and modifying still images

> Get started with the Generate panel — choose a model, write a prompt, generate a first image, and send results to the Gallery or the Canvas.

The **Generate** panel is where you create still images from a text prompt. This page gets you started: choosing a model, writing a prompt and generating a first image, and choosing whether results go to the Gallery or the Canvas. The [Generate Panel Reference](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/) then describes every section of the panel in detail. The Generate panel sits in the left rail of the **Compose** layout (**Alt+1**), where finished images appear in the Preview in the center of the screen. It is also in the **Edit** layout (**Alt+2**), next to the Canvas. Press **1** to bring it to the front, or **Alt+A** to jump straight to its prompt. See [The Workbench](/users-guide/workbench/introduction/) for how layouts and panels work. The panel is divided into sections: the model picker and prompts at the top, followed by **Size**, **Guidance**, **Render**, **Components** and **Advanced**. Which sections and fields you see depends on the selected model, and each section header shows a summary of its settings, so you can keep sections you rarely change collapsed. ![The Generate panel with an SDXL model selected, a prompt and negative prompt entered, one concept added, and the Size, Guidance and Render sections open.](/_astro/generate-panel-overview.BA34WKOD_25kQEs.webp) ## Selecting a model [Section titled “Selecting a model”](#selecting-a-model) The **Model** picker at the top of the panel lists the image generation models you have installed, grouped by model family. Type in **Search models…** to find one by name, family or description, or use the family chips to narrow the list. If the list is empty, install a model first; see [Managing media generation models](/users-guide/models/introduction/). When you switch models, the panel keeps your prompt and settings and adjusts only what the new model cannot use: it snaps the size to the new model’s grid, and turns off or removes concepts, reference images and options the model does not support. If anything would be lost, a **Switch model?** dialog lists it before you confirm. Switching does not load the new model’s recommended settings; use [Reset all to model defaults](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#resetting-to-defaults) for that. ### Model components [Section titled “Model components”](#model-components) Many newer models are installed as a single file that holds only the main network, and need companion models, such as a text encoder and a VAE, to generate. For these models the panel shows a **Components** section with a slot for each companion model. A Diffusers install of the same model carries its own components and leaves the slots on **Model default**. [Submodels](/users-guide/models/model-families/#submodels) explains what each component does, and each model family’s page under [Local Models](/users-guide/models/model-families/#model-families) lists the ones it needs. If a required component is missing, **Invoke** is disabled and its tooltip names the slot to fill, for example *“Generate needs a VAE for FLUX models.”* Pick an installed model in the slot, or install the family’s starter bundle from the Model Manager, which includes everything the family needs. ## Your first image [Section titled “Your first image”](#your-first-image) 1. **Write a prompt.** Type a description of the image into the **Prompt** box, for example *a lighthouse on a rocky coast at sunset, dramatic clouds, oil painting*. Describe the subject, the setting, the lighting and the style you want. The [Prompting Guide](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/) has advice on writing prompts that work. 2. **Choose how many images.** The **Iterations** field in the top bar, next to **Invoke**, sets how many images one press of Invoke produces. [Seed](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#seed) explains how their seeds are chosen. 3. **Press Invoke** in the top bar, or press **Ctrl+Enter** (**Cmd+Enter** on macOS). The job joins the queue, and the top bar shows its progress. The first run with a model takes longer while the model loads. 4. **See the result.** The finished image appears in the Preview and is saved to the Gallery. To stop a run, click the cancel button in the queue area of the top bar, or press **Shift+X**. Hover over **Invoke** to see what will be queued, for example *1 prompt × 4 iterations → 4 generations*. When Invoke is disabled, the same tooltip lists what is stopping it. ## Routing images to the Gallery or the Canvas [Section titled “Routing images to the Gallery or the Canvas”](#routing-images-to-the-gallery-or-the-canvas) Every press of **Invoke** has a *route*: a **source**, the panel whose settings are used, and a **destination**, where the results go. Images can go to one of two destinations: * **Gallery** — the image is saved to the Gallery, on the board selected there, and shown in the Preview. * **Canvas** — the image lands in the Canvas’s staging area, where you can compare the results and accept one onto the canvas as a new layer. Each layout preset starts with the route that suits its purpose. The **Compose** preset routes the Generate panel to the **Gallery**. The **Edit** preset routes to the **Canvas**, using the Canvas’s layers and bounding box as the source, so results come back to the canvas for further editing. Switching presets switches to the new preset’s route, unless the routing is locked. The routing control next to **Invoke** in the top bar shows the current source and destination as a pair of icons. Click it to change either one: * **Source** lists the panels in the current layout that can run a generation, such as Generate, Canvas, Upscale and Video. * **Destination** chooses **Gallery** or **Canvas**. * **Lock routing** keeps the route fixed. A small dot on the control shows that it is locked. ![The routing menu next to Invoke, with Source (Generate, Canvas, Upscale, Video, Workflow), Destination (Canvas or Gallery) and Lock routing.](/_astro/routing-menu.BsA5Ukno_Z2nDCu8.webp) The route also follows your work. When you change a setting in a different panel, that panel becomes the source, and the destination changes to match: the Canvas sends results to the Canvas, and the other panels send them to the Gallery. For example, editing the prompt in the Generate panel while you are in the Edit layout sends the next results to the Gallery. Lock the routing if you want results to keep going to one place while you work in several panels. To send a single run to the other destination without changing the route, press **Alt+Ctrl+Enter** (**Alt+Cmd+Enter** on macOS). The route is saved with the project, so each project remembers where its results go. See [Projects](/users-guide/projects/introduction/#what-a-project-keeps) for everything a project keeps. ## Going further [Section titled “Going further”](#going-further) The [Generate Panel Reference](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/) describes the rest of the panel in detail: * **[Image size](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#setting-the-image-size)** — width, height, aspect ratio and the model’s optimal size. * **[Render settings](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#render-settings)** — steps, CFG or guidance, scheduler, seed, the negative prompt, advanced options, and **Reset all to model defaults**. * **[Concepts](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#adding-concepts)** — add LoRAs that teach the model a style, character or object. * **[Reference images](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#adding-reference-images)** — guide the image by example instead of by words. * **[Prompt tools](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#prompt-tools)** — expand a prompt, write one from an image, and reuse earlier prompts. The [Prompting Guide](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/) covers writing prompts that work, prompt templates and dynamic prompts.

# Parameter Selection Guide

> How to choose steps, CFG or guidance, schedulers, seeds, size and denoising strength for the model you are using, with a historical study of sampler convergence.

The right settings depend far more on the model than on any general rule. This guide explains how to choose them, starting from the model’s own recommendations. For where each setting lives in the Generate panel, see [Render settings](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#render-settings). ## Start from the model’s defaults [Section titled “Start from the model’s defaults”](#start-from-the-models-defaults) Each model has recommended settings, which are shown as marks on the sliders and which you can edit in the Model Manager. When you change models, InvokeAI keeps your current settings if they are compatible, so after switching models click **Reset all to model defaults** (the ↺ button in the Generate panel’s title bar) to start from the new model’s recommendations. Each model family’s page under [Local Models](/users-guide/models/model-families/#model-families) lists its typical values. ## Steps [Section titled “Steps”](#steps) More steps refine an image up to a point; beyond it, an image changes little and generation only takes longer. * **Distilled models** — Turbo, Lightning and Schnell variants, and models used with a Lightning or Turbo LoRA — are trained for a specific small number of steps, typically 4 to 10. Using many more does not help and can make results worse. * **Standard models** usually need 25 to 50 steps. SD 1.5 and SDXL work well at about 30. * To explore ideas quickly, generate a batch at fewer steps, then recall the seed of the image you like and generate it again at the full step count (see [Seeds](#seeds) below). ## CFG and guidance [Section titled “CFG and guidance”](#cfg-and-guidance) **CFG** sets how strictly the model follows the prompt. Higher values follow it more literally but look harsher; lower values are looser and more natural. * SD 1.5 and SDXL: about 5 to 8. * Newer standard models, such as SD 3.5, Qwen Image, ERNIE-Image and Krea-2 Raw: about 3.5 to 6. * Distilled models: 1. At a CFG of 1 the negative prompt has no effect, so several model families hide or ignore it. * FLUX.1 and some other families show **Guidance** instead, a value built into the model; about 3.5 for FLUX.1 dev. If an image looks oversaturated or “burned”, lower CFG; if it ignores parts of the prompt, raise it slightly or improve the prompt. ## Schedulers [Section titled “Schedulers”](#schedulers) The scheduler decides how much noise is removed at each step. Which ones are offered depends on the model: * **SD 1.5, SD 2.x and SDXL** offer the full list. **DPM++ 2M Karras** and **Euler** are good general-purpose choices; **Euler Ancestral** and the other *Ancestral* and *SDE* schedulers add variety and keep changing the image as steps increase; **UniPC** and **DPM++ 3M** reach good results in fewer steps. **LCM** and **TCD** are only for LCM- and TCD-distilled models. * **Flow models**, such as FLUX.1, FLUX.2, Z-Image and ERNIE-Image, offer **Euler**, **Heun (2nd order)**, which is slower per step but can need fewer steps, and **LCM** for distilled models. * **Anima** has its own short list, starting with **Euler**. * Some families, including SD 3.5, Qwen Image, CogView4, Krea-2 and Ideogram 4, use a fixed schedule and do not show the field. **Use model default scheduler** switches back to the model’s own choice. ## Seeds [Section titled “Seeds”](#seeds) The seed sets the starting noise, so the same model, prompt, seed and settings reproduce the same image. * While exploring, leave **Seed mode** on **Random** to get a different image every time. * To refine a result, set the seed to **Fixed**, for example by clicking the image’s thumbnail under **Recent seeds**, and then change one setting at a time so you can see exactly what it does. * To polish a promising draft, recall its seed with **Use Seed** from the image’s **Recall Metadata** menu and generate it again at more steps or a larger size. ## Size [Section titled “Size”](#size) Each model has an optimal image area, around one megapixel for most current models and less for SD 1.5. Results are best near that size; much larger images can repeat subjects or distort anatomy. Use **Set optimal size** in the Size section, and upscale afterwards for larger images. ## Denoising strength [Section titled “Denoising strength”](#denoising-strength) For image-to-image, inpainting and outpainting on the Canvas, **Denoising strength** sets how much the existing image may change. Around 30% to 50% keeps the composition and colors while changing details; 70% and above (the default is 75%) reworks the image substantially, keeping only its broad layout. ## Appendix: sampler convergence on SD 1.x (historical) [Section titled “Appendix: sampler convergence on SD 1.x (historical)”](#appendix-sampler-convergence-on-sd-1x-historical) Summary * Results converge as steps are increased, except with the ancestral samplers (`K_DPM_2_A` and `K_EULER_A`). Often at 100 steps or more, but sometimes not until 700. * Producing a batch of candidate images at low step counts (8 to 30) can save hours of computation. * `K_HEUN` and `K_DPM_2` converge in fewer steps, but are slower per step. * `K_DPM_2_A` and `K_EULER_A` incorporate a lot of creativity and variability. ### Sampler speed [Section titled “Sampler speed”](#sampler-speed) *(Tested on an M1 Max with 64 GB, at 512×512, averaged over 3 samples.)* | Sampler | it/s | | :---------- | :----------------- | | `DDIM` | 1.89 | | `PLMS` | 1.86 | | `K_EULER` | 1.86 | | `K_LMS` | **1.91** (fastest) | | `K_EULER_A` | 1.86 | | `K_HEUN` | 0.95 *(slower)* | | `K_DPM_2` | 0.95 *(slower)* | | `K_DPM_2_A` | 0.95 *(slower)* | ### Sampler Results by Subject [Section titled “Sampler Results by Subject”](#sampler-results-by-subject) Let’s start by choosing a prompt and using it with each of our 8 samplers, running it for 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 100 steps. #### Anime [Section titled “Anime”](#anime) > `"an anime girl" -W512 -H512 -C7.5 -S3031912972` ![Anime Comparison Grid](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/191868725-7f7af991-e254-4c1f-83e7-bed8c9b2d34f.png) Immediately, you can notice results tend to converge — that is, as `-s` (step) values increase, images look more and more similar until there comes a point where the image no longer changes. You can also notice how `DDIM` and `PLMS` eventually tend to converge to K-sampler results as steps are increased. Among K-samplers, `K_HEUN` and `K_DPM_2` seem to require the fewest steps to converge, and even at low step counts they are good indicators of the final result. Finally, `K_DPM_2_A` and `K_EULER_A` seem to do a bit of their own thing and don’t keep much similarity with the rest of the samplers. #### Nature [Section titled “Nature”](#nature) Now, these results seem interesting, but do they hold for other topics? Let’s try! > `"valley landscape wallpaper, d&d art, fantasy, painted, 4k, high detail, sharp focus, washed colors, elaborate excellent painted illustration" -W512 -H512 -C7.5 -S1458228930` ![Nature Comparison Grid](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/191868763-b151c69e-0a72-4cf1-a151-5a64edd0c93e.png) With nature, you can see how initial results are even more indicative of the final result — more so than with characters/people. `K_HEUN` and `K_DPM_2` are again the quickest indicators, almost right from the start. Results also converge faster (e.g. `K_HEUN` converged at `-s21`). #### Food [Section titled “Food”](#food) > `"a hamburger with a bowl of french fries" -W512 -H512 -C7.5 -S4053222918` ![Food Comparison Grid](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/191868898-98801a62-885f-4ea1-aee8-563503522aa9.png) Again, `K_HEUN` and `K_DPM_2` take the fewest number of steps to be good indicators of the final result. `K_DPM_2_A` and `K_EULER_A` seem to incorporate a lot of creativity/variability, capable of producing rotten hamburgers, but also of adding lettuce to the mix. And they’re the only samplers that produced an actual ‘bowl of fries’! #### Animals [Section titled “Animals”](#animals) > `"grown tiger, full body" -W512 -H512 -C7.5 -S3721629802` ![Animal Comparison Grid](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/191868870-9e3b7d82-b909-429f-893a-13f6ec343454.png) `K_HEUN` and `K_DPM_2` once again require the least number of steps to be indicative of the final result (around `-s30`), while other samplers are still struggling with several tails or malformed back legs. It also takes longer to converge (for comparison, `K_HEUN` required around 150 steps to converge). This is normal, as producing human/animal faces/bodies is one of the things the model struggles the most with. For these topics, running for more steps will often increase coherence within the composition. #### People [Section titled “People”](#people) > `"Ultra realistic photo, (Miranda Bloom-Kerr), young, stunning model, blue eyes, blond hair, beautiful face, intricate, highly detailed, smooth, art by artgerm and greg rutkowski and alphonse mucha, stained glass" -W512 -H512 -C7.5 -S2131956332`. *(This time, we will go up to 300 steps).* ![People Comparison Grid 1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/191871743-6802f199-0ffd-4986-98c5-df2d8db30d18.png) Observing the results, it again takes longer for all samplers to converge (`K_HEUN` took around 150 steps), but we can observe good indicative results much earlier (see: `K_HEUN`). Conversely, `DDIM` and `PLMS` are still undergoing moderate changes (see: lace around her neck), even at `-s300`. In fact, as we can see in this other experiment, some samplers can take 700+ steps to converge when generating people. ![People Comparison Grid 2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/191992123-7e0759d6-6220-42c4-a961-88c7071c5ee6.png) Note also the point of convergence may not be the most desirable state (e.g. you might prefer an earlier version of the face that is more rounded), but it will probably be the most coherent regarding arms/hands/face attributes. You can always merge different images with a photo editing tool and pass it through `img2img` to smoothen the composition. *** ### Batch Generation Speedup [Section titled “Batch Generation Speedup”](#batch-generation-speedup) This realization about convergence is very useful because it means you don’t need to create a batch of 100 images (`-n100`) at `-s100` just to choose your favorite 2 or 3 images. You can produce the same 100 images at `-s10` to `-s30` using a K-sampler (since they converge faster), get a rough idea of the final result, choose your 2 or 3 favorite ones, and then run `-s100` on those specific images to polish details. This technique is **3-8x as quick**. ### Three Key Takeaways [Section titled “Three Key Takeaways”](#three-key-takeaways) Finally, it is relevant to mention that, in general, there are 3 important moments in the process of image formation as steps increase: 1. **The Indicator Stage:** The earliest point at which an image becomes a good indicator of the final result. This is useful for batch generation at low step values to preview outputs before committing to higher steps. 2. **The Coherence Stage:** The point at which an image becomes coherent, even if different from the final converged result. This is useful for low-step batch generation where quality is improved via other techniques (like inpainting) rather than raw step count. 3. **The Convergence Stage:** The point at which an image fully converges and stops changing. ![Low Step Sampler Comparison](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50542132/192046823-2714cb29-bbf3-4eb1-9213-e27a0963905c.png)

# Prompt Tools

The prompt toolbar holds tools that help you write prompts. **Expand Prompt** and **Image to Prompt** use local language models to write or rewrite a prompt for you; if no compatible model is installed, the tool’s popover says so and offers an **Open Model Manager** button. **Prompt triggers** insert the trigger phrases, embeddings and wildcards your models need. ## Expand Prompt [Section titled “Expand Prompt”](#expand-prompt) Takes your short prompt and expands it into a detailed, vivid description suitable for image generation. **How to use:** 1. Type a brief prompt (e.g. “a cat in a garden”) 2. Click **Expand prompt** (the pencil-and-sparkles button) in the prompt toolbar 3. Select a Text LLM model from the dropdown. The panel remembers your choice for the project. 4. Choose a **System prompt**, the instructions that tell the model how to rewrite your prompt 5. Click **Expand** 6. Your prompt is replaced with the expanded version, which you can edit before generating ### System prompts [Section titled “System prompts”](#system-prompts) InvokeAI ships with a **Default** system prompt and several tuned for particular model families, such as FLUX.2, Z-Image, Qwen Image and Krea-2. To add your own, click the gear button next to the System prompt selector (**Manage system prompts**) and choose **New**. A system prompt has a **Name**, the **Instructions** given to the language model, and an optional **Max output length** in tokens (300 by default). You can duplicate, edit and delete your own system prompts. Shared system prompts, including the built-in ones, are marked **Shared**. On a multi-user installation only administrators can edit them, and changes apply to every user. **Compatible models:** Any HuggingFace model with a `ForCausalLM` architecture, plus Gemma-4 checkpoints (`Gemma4ForConditionalGeneration`), which can also read an image. Recommended options: | Model | Size | HuggingFace ID | | --------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------ | | Qwen2.5 1.5B Instruct | \~3 GB | `Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` | | Phi-3 Mini Instruct | \~7.5 GB | `microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct` | | TinyLlama Chat | \~2 GB | `TinyLlama/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0` | Install by pasting the HuggingFace ID into the Model Manager. The model is automatically detected as a **Text LLM** type. ### Prompt enhancement for LTX-2.5 [Section titled “Prompt enhancement for LTX-2.5”](#prompt-enhancement-for-ltx-25) LTX-2.5 was trained on long, single-paragraph audio-visual captions, and its own text encoder is not trained to write them. Lightricks pairs the model with a small dedicated enhancer, and InvokeAI offers the same pairing through Expand Prompt: * Install **LTX-2.5 Prompt Enhancer (Gemma-4 E2B)** from the starter models (`google/gemma-4-E2B-it`, \~10 GB). It is optional and not part of the LTX-2.5 bundle. * Two system prompts ship with InvokeAI: **LTX-2.5 Text-to-Video** and **LTX-2.5 Image-to-Video**, the release’s own texts. In the Video panel with an LTX-2 model selected, Expand Prompt preselects the enhancer — when it was installed from the starter models or as `google/gemma-4-E2B-it`; otherwise the popover points you to the starter models — and the matching system prompt. With a **first frame** set it shows the frame with **Describe from the first frame** ticked and uses the Image-to-Video prompt, so the caption begins from what the image shows. Untick it, or pick a model that cannot read images (the popover says so), and it uses the Text-to-Video prompt instead. Any model or system prompt you choose in the popover overrides the suggestion. The rewritten prompt replaces yours in the prompt box, where you can edit it before pressing Invoke; the prompt that is generated and recorded is exactly what the box holds. ### Reasoning (“thinking”) models [Section titled “Reasoning (“thinking”) models”](#reasoning-thinking-models) Reasoning models such as Qwen3 or the DeepSeek-R1 distills normally write out a chain of thought before their answer. Prompt expansion returns the generated text as-is, so that reasoning would end up in your prompt. InvokeAI therefore renders the chat template with thinking disabled, which makes these models answer directly. Models whose chat template does not support the switch are unaffected, and models that always reason (with no way to turn it off) are not suitable for prompt expansion. ## Image to Prompt [Section titled “Image to Prompt”](#image-to-prompt) Upload an image and generate a descriptive prompt from it using a vision-language model. **How to use:** 1. Select an image in the Gallery or Preview, or drag an image from the Gallery onto the prompt box (**Describe this image**), which opens the tool for you 2. Click **Image to prompt** in the prompt toolbar if it is not already open 3. Select a LLaVA OneVision model from the dropdown 4. Click **Generate Prompt** 5. The generated description replaces your prompt **Compatible models:** LLaVA OneVision models (already supported by InvokeAI). ## Replacing your prompt [Section titled “Replacing your prompt”](#replacing-your-prompt) Both tools replace the text in the prompt box. To get an earlier prompt back, open **Prompt history** in the prompt toolbar: every prompt you have submitted with Invoke is kept there. ## Prompt triggers [Section titled “Prompt triggers”](#prompt-triggers) Some models only produce their effect when the prompt contains a particular word or phrase. A LoRA trained on a character may need the character’s name; a style LoRA may need a keyword such as `pixel art style`. These **trigger phrases** are easy to forget, so InvokeAI collects them, together with embeddings and wildcards, in a menu you can insert from while writing a prompt. ### Inserting a trigger [Section titled “Inserting a trigger”](#inserting-a-trigger) Click the **+** button in the prompt toolbar (**Add prompt trigger**). It is available on the positive and negative prompts in the Generate, Video and Upscale panels. The menu lists, in this order: | Group | What it contains | Inserted as | | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------ | | **Wildcards** | Your [wildcards](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/#wildcards) (positive prompt only). | `__name__` | | *The selected main model’s name* | The main model’s trigger phrases. | the phrase | | *Each enabled concept’s name* | The trigger phrases of each LoRA that is switched on in the Guidance section. Disabled concepts are skipped. | the phrase | | **Compatible embeddings** | Every installed embedding (textual inversion) that works with the selected main model. | `<embedding-name>` | Type in **Search prompt triggers** to filter the list, then click an item. It is inserted at the cursor exactly as shown, without extra spaces or commas, so add any separators you need. If the menu is empty, none of your installed models have trigger phrases and no embeddings or wildcards are available. The **Open Model Manager** button takes you to where trigger phrases are set. The **+** button is disabled while you are previewing the merged prompt of a [template](/users-guide/image-generation/prompting-guide/#prompt-templates). Two kinds of triggers can also be completed as you type: * Type `<` in either prompt to list compatible **embeddings**. * Type `__` (two underscores) in the positive prompt to list **wildcards**. Use the arrow keys to choose, **Enter** or **Tab** to insert, and **Escape** to close the list. Trigger phrases of models and LoRAs are only offered in the **+** menu. ### Defining trigger phrases [Section titled “Defining trigger phrases”](#defining-trigger-phrases) Trigger phrases belong to a model and are set in the **Model Manager**. Select a main model or a LoRA and find the **Trigger Phrases** field in its detail view. Type a phrase and press **Enter** to add it; each phrase can be up to 200 characters, and duplicates are refused. Changes are saved as you make them. Trigger phrases come from the model’s creator, so check the model’s download page (Civitai or HuggingFace) for the words it expects. Two things fill them in for you: * When you install a LoRA that has a companion `.json` file next to it with an `activation text` entry, as some download tools create, those phrases become the LoRA’s trigger phrases. * Trigger phrases are included when you [export and import a model’s settings](/users-guide/models/introduction/#exporting-and-importing-model-settings). The Guidance section of the Generate panel shows each LoRA’s trigger phrases under its name as a reminder. Adding a LoRA does not insert them into your prompt; use the **+** menu for that. ## Text LLM workflow nodes [Section titled “Text LLM workflow nodes”](#text-llm-workflow-nodes) The workflow editor provides **Text LLM** and **Text LLM (with System Prompt Preset)** nodes for automated pipelines. Both accept a prompt, model, maximum token count, and seed, then output generated text as a string. The preset variant reads its system prompt from the System Prompts library. Using the same seed reproduces sampling when the model, prompt, settings, hardware, and software versions remain the same. Results may differ across devices or software versions. The prompt area’s **Expand Prompt** tool chooses a fresh seed for each request so repeated expansions can vary. API callers can pass an optional seed to **Expand Prompt**; the response returns the effective seed for replay. They can also pass an `image_name` to condition the rewrite on a stored image, which requires a Text LLM whose `supports_images` is true. When a saved `1.0.0` Text LLM workflow is migrated, its new seed defaults to `0`, so repeated runs become deterministic. Connect a random integer node to **seed** if the workflow should vary between runs.

# Prompting Guide

> Write prompts that work, then go further with prompt templates, dynamic prompts and wildcards.

The prompt is your main way of telling a model what to create. This guide starts with writing good prompts, which is all most images need. It then covers the tools that save typing and add variety: prompt templates, dynamic prompts and wildcards. [Advanced Prompt Syntax](/users-guide/image-generation/advanced-prompt-syntax/) covers the syntax for fine control. For the tools that write or rewrite a prompt for you, **Expand prompt** and **Image to prompt**, and for inserting trigger phrases, see [Prompt Tools](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/). ## Writing a prompt [Section titled “Writing a prompt”](#writing-a-prompt) Prompting works best when you describe the image clearly, then refine only the parts that matter. Most good prompts cover a few of these: Subject Start with the main thing you want to see: a character, object, scene, or action. Style or Medium Add the visual language: photograph, watercolor, oil painting, 3D render, anime illustration, and so on. Lighting and Composition Describe the camera angle, framing, lighting, environment, color palette, or mood that will shape the image. Detail and Finish Add a few high-value details such as fabric texture, shallow depth of field, natural skin texture, or painterly brushwork. A simple pattern that works well is: `subject, style or medium, lighting or composition, a few important details` Not every prompt needs every category. Start simple, then add detail only when the model needs more direction. ### Positive and negative prompts [Section titled “Positive and negative prompts”](#positive-and-negative-prompts) The **positive prompt** describes what you want the model to create. Put the most important idea early and keep the wording concrete. The **negative prompt** lists what you do not want. Use it to remove recurring problems or unwanted traits, and keep it short and targeted rather than pasting a giant list into every generation. Good negative prompts name specific failure modes: `blurry`, `distorted hands`, `low detail`, `extra limbs`. Not every model uses a negative prompt. See [Negative prompt](/users-guide/image-generation/generate-panel/#negative-prompt) in the Generate panel guide for which models do. ### A practical workflow [Section titled “A practical workflow”](#a-practical-workflow) 1. **Start with the core image.** Write the clearest version of the image you want before adding stylistic extras. 2. **Add style and composition.** Once the subject is right, add medium, lens, lighting, mood, background, or framing details. 3. **Test with a fixed seed.** When you are learning what a prompt change does, set the seed mode to **Fixed** so you can compare results directly. 4. **Change one thing at a time.** If you add five new terms at once, you will not know which one helped. 5. **Escalate only when needed.** If the result is close but one element is too weak or too strong, use [attention weighting](/users-guide/image-generation/advanced-prompt-syntax/#attention-weighting). If you want lots of variations, use [dynamic prompts](#dynamic-prompts). Here is the same idea refined in stages: 
```text
portrait of a woman


portrait of a woman, studio photograph, soft key light


portrait of a woman, studio photograph, soft key light, 85mm lens, shallow depth of field, natural skin texture
```
 ### Write for the model you are using [Section titled “Write for the model you are using”](#write-for-the-model-you-are-using) The same prompt can behave very differently across models. * Newer models with large language-model text encoders, such as FLUX, Qwen Image, Z-Image and Krea-2, understand full sentences and long, detailed descriptions. Describe the scene as you would to a person, including how things relate to each other and any text that should appear in the image. * Older models such as SD 1.5 and SDXL use CLIP text encoders trained on short captions, and respond best to short, comma-separated phrases. * Photo-oriented models respond well to camera, lens, lighting and texture language. Illustration models often respond better to medium, art direction and shape language. * Specialty models and concepts may expect specific [trigger phrases](/users-guide/image-generation/prompt-tools/#prompt-triggers) from their model card. * If a prompt works beautifully on one model and poorly on another, that does not always mean the prompt is bad. The model may just speak a different visual language. ### Common mistakes [Section titled “Common mistakes”](#common-mistakes) * Packing too many unrelated ideas into one prompt. * Using long generic quality-word lists before you know the base prompt works. * Treating the negative prompt as a trash can for every bad outcome. * Expecting identical behavior across models, schedulers, and workflows. * Changing prompt, model, seed, and settings all at once while troubleshooting. ### Example prompts [Section titled “Example prompts”](#example-prompts) **Photographic portrait** 
```text
editorial portrait of a woman in a charcoal coat, studio photograph, soft key light, subtle rim light, 85mm lens, shallow depth of field, natural skin texture
```
 Negative: `blurry, low detail, waxy skin, extra fingers` **Environment concept art** 
```text
ancient stone temple built into a cliffside, fantasy concept art, misty sunrise, towering scale, moss-covered stairs, cinematic atmosphere
```
 Negative: `flat lighting, low contrast, muddy details` **Product-style render** 
```text
sleek ceramic teapot on a matte stone surface, product photography, clean studio lighting, soft shadow, high detail, minimal background
```
 Negative: `cluttered background, distortion, duplicate objects` **Stylized illustration** 
```text
fox courier crossing a rainy city street, storybook illustration, bold shapes, glowing shop signs, reflective pavement, warm and cool color contrast
```
 Negative: `photorealistic, dull colors, low detail` ## Prompt templates [Section titled “Prompt templates”](#prompt-templates) A prompt template is a reusable piece of prompt text, such as a photographic or artistic style, that wraps whatever you type. Apply **Photography (General)** once, and every prompt you write is sent as a photograph without you retyping the style words. Templates are available in the **Generate** panel. ### Applying a template [Section titled “Applying a template”](#applying-a-template) Click **Templates** in the positive prompt’s toolbar. The popover lists the templates available to you in three groups: * **Your templates** — templates you have created.
