# Custom Node Manager

The Custom Node Manager installs, updates, and removes community node packs directly from the InvokeAI UI — no manual file copying, no restart required. ## Opening the Custom Node Manager [Section titled “Opening the Custom Node Manager”](#opening-the-custom-node-manager) Click the **Nodes** tab (circuit icon) in the left sidebar, between **Models** and **Queue**. The page is split into two panels: * **Left:** the list of installed node packs, with each pack’s node count, type badges, and on-disk path. * **Right:** the install UI, with tabs for **Git Repository URL** and **Scan Folder**, plus an install log at the bottom. ## Installing a node pack [Section titled “Installing a node pack”](#installing-a-node-pack) 1. On the right panel, choose the **Git Repository URL** tab. 2. Paste the Git URL of the pack, e.g. `https://github.com/user/my-node-pack.git`. 3. Click **Install**. What happens during install: * The repo is cloned into your `nodes` directory. * The nodes are loaded into the running InvokeAI process immediately — **no restart needed**. * Any workflow `.json` files found in the repo are imported into your workflow library and tagged with `node-pack:<pack-name>` so you can filter for them. * The install log at the bottom of the panel shows the result for each step. Security Custom nodes execute arbitrary Python on your machine. **Only install node packs from authors you trust.** A malicious pack could harm your system or exfiltrate data. ### Python dependencies [Section titled “Python dependencies”](#python-dependencies) The Custom Node Manager **does not** automatically run `pip install` for a pack’s `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`. Auto-installing into the running InvokeAI environment risks pulling in incompatible package versions and breaking the application. If a pack ships extra dependencies, you’ll see a warning toast after installation. Install them yourself — typically `pip install -r requirements.txt` from inside an activated InvokeAI environment, but check the pack’s README first. After installing, click **Reload** so the new dependencies take effect. ## Managing installed packs [Section titled “Managing installed packs”](#managing-installed-packs) Each entry in the left panel has actions for managing the pack: * **Reload** — re-scans the `nodes` directory. Use this after manually adding a pack via `git clone`, or after installing extra Python dependencies. * **Uninstall** — removes the pack from disk, unregisters its nodes from the running process, and removes any workflows that were imported from the pack. No restart needed. ## Scan Folder tab [Section titled “Scan Folder tab”](#scan-folder-tab) The **Scan Folder** tab shows the path of your `nodes` directory. Anything placed there manually (for example, by `git clone`-ing a pack directly) is detected automatically at startup. Use **Reload** to pick up packs added at runtime. ## Troubleshooting [Section titled “Troubleshooting”](#troubleshooting) ### Install fails [Section titled “Install fails”](#install-fails) * Confirm the Git URL is correct and reachable. * The repo must contain an `__init__.py` at its root. * Read the install log — it surfaces the underlying error. ### Nodes don’t appear after install [Section titled “Nodes don’t appear after install”](#nodes-dont-appear-after-install) * Click **Reload**. * Check that the pack’s `__init__.py` imports the node classes. * Check the server console for import errors. ### Workflows show errors after uninstalling [Section titled “Workflows show errors after uninstalling”](#workflows-show-errors-after-uninstalling) User-created workflows that reference nodes from an uninstalled pack will show errors for the missing node types. Either reinstall the pack or remove the affected nodes from the workflow. ## Authoring a node pack [Section titled “Authoring a node pack”](#authoring-a-node-pack) If you want to publish your own pack so it can be installed by URL, see the [Creating a Node Pack](/development/guides/creating-nodes/) developer guide for the required repository layout, `__init__.py` requirements, and conventions for shipping workflows alongside your nodes.

# Workflow Editor Reference

> Details of the workflow editor — adding and connecting nodes, connectors, which results reach the Gallery, managing workflows and the library, common node patterns, community nodes and keyboard shortcuts.

This page describes working in the workflow editor in detail. For an introduction to workflows, a tour of the editor and a step-by-step walkthrough, see [Automating with Workflows](/users-guide/workflows/introduction/). ## Working in the editor [Section titled “Working in the editor”](#working-in-the-editor) ### Adding and connecting nodes [Section titled “Adding and connecting nodes”](#adding-and-connecting-nodes) To add a node, press **Shift+A** or **Space** in the editor, or click **+** (**Add node**) in the editor’s header. Type to search: every word you type must appear in the node’s name, type, tags or category. Nodes are grouped by category, each with a short description and the node pack it comes from; nodes still in development are marked with a hammer icon (*Beta*). Click a node to add it near the middle of the view. ![The node picker searching for "compositor", showing the Image Compositor node in the Image category.](/_astro/workflow-node-picker.Ctpk2pH0_Z1bEUlx.webp) A quicker way to add a node that is already connected: drag from a connection point and release it over empty space. The picker opens showing only the nodes that can connect to that point, and the new node is wired up for you. To connect two nodes, drag from an output on the right of one node to an input on the left of another. Only compatible connection points accept the connection. An input takes one connection, but an output can feed as many inputs as you like. To reconnect, drag the end of a connection to another point; to disconnect, drag it away and release it over empty space, or select the connection and press **Delete**. Right-click a node to **Copy**, **Paste**, **Duplicate**, **Collapse** or **Delete** it, and double-click its title to rename it. The chevron in a node’s title bar collapses it to keep a large graph tidy. The picker’s **Utility** group has three special nodes: * **Notes** — a sticky note for explaining a workflow to others, or to yourself later. * **Current Image** — shows the image being generated and the latest result, for keeping an eye on long workflows. * **Connector** — a small dot for rerouting connections (see below). #### Connectors [Section titled “Connectors”](#connectors) Connectors tidy up the wiring of a large graph. They pass a value straight through and are removed before the workflow runs, so they cannot change what it does. To add one, right-click empty space in the editor and choose **Add connector**, then connect to and from it. You can wire a connector’s output first and its input later; it only accepts a source whose type matches what it feeds. Deleting a connector joins its incoming connection directly to everything it fed. A node’s border shows its state: red when a required input is missing or the node failed, highlighted with a progress strip while it runs, and green when it has finished. After a run, **Latest output** on an image node shows its result. ### Where results go [Section titled “Where results go”](#where-results-go) Only nodes whose **Save to Gallery** box is checked, at the bottom of nodes that produce images, send their images to the Gallery. The images of other nodes are intermediate results that are used and then discarded. New nodes start with **Save to Gallery** turned off, so check it on the node that makes your final image. An image node’s **Board** field chooses where its saved images go. **Auto**, the default, uses the Gallery’s destination: the selected board, or the auto-add board if one is set (see [Choosing where new media goes](/users-guide/gallery/introduction/#choosing-where-new-media-goes)). **None** saves to Uncategorized, and you can also pick a specific board. Images from nodes that have no Board field go to Uncategorized. Beside it, **Use cache** lets InvokeAI reuse a node’s previous result when its inputs have not changed, which speeds up repeated runs. On a multi-user installation, only administrators see this option. ### Your workflows [Section titled “Your workflows”](#your-workflows) Each project keeps its own workflows, and one of them is **active**: the one shown in the editor and run by Invoke. Changes are saved with the project automatically. Click the workflow’s name to open the **Workflows** library: * **This project** — the project’s workflows. Open one to make it active, or start a **New workflow**. * **Browse** — the workflows that ship with InvokeAI, such as *Text to Image - SDXL*, *Flux Text to Image* and the video workflows. Opening one adds a copy to your project. * **Yours** — workflows you have saved to your library with **Save to library…**, for use in other projects. Opening a library workflow adds an independent copy to the project; the library’s version is untouched. If the project already has a copy, opening the template asks what to do: **Open copy** switches to the existing copy, **Add new copy** makes another one, and **Replace copy** replaces the copy’s graph with the library version while keeping its name. A replace can be undone in one step. Changes to a project’s workflows never change the library by themselves. **Save to library…**, in the editor’s header, saves the workflow as a new library template with the name you give it, including its form and its current settings as defaults. For a workflow opened from one of your own templates, **Update library template** replaces that template instead. If the template has changed since you opened it, you can save as a new template instead, or review the current one and replace it deliberately. Replacing a template also affects workflows that use it through the **Call Saved Workflow** node. Add comma-separated tags, such as `portrait, SDXL, upscaling`, in the workflow’s **Details**; they become filters in the library. Each workflow also keeps its own undo history while the project is open. To share a workflow, use **Export workflow JSON** from the **⋯** menu; others can load it with **Import workflow JSON…**. An image made by a workflow also carries the workflow in its metadata: right-click the image and choose **Load Workflow**. **Download workflow as PNG** in the editor toolbar saves a picture of the whole graph, at up to twice screen resolution, for documentation or sharing. A large graph is saved at a lower resolution, with a notice when that falls below screen resolution; one too large to stay legible as a picture is not exported, so share its JSON instead. Closing the workflow editor while the picture is being prepared cancels the export. ## Common node patterns [Section titled “Common node patterns”](#common-node-patterns) A few groups of nodes appear in almost every image workflow. Knowing what they do makes it easier to read the bundled workflows and to build your own. * **Model, prompts and denoising.** A model loader, such as **Main Model - SDXL**, provides the model’s parts: the UNet or transformer that denoises, the text encoders (CLIP) and the VAE. Prompt nodes turn text into *conditioning* using the text encoders. The denoise node needs both positive and negative conditioning, even if the negative prompt is empty. * **Noise and seeds.** Text-to-image starts from random noise, made by **Create Latent Noise** from a **Seed**, **Width** and **Height**. Its **Noise Type** must match the model family: **SD** for SD 1.5 and SDXL, or the matching family for FLUX, FLUX.2, SD3, CogView4, Z-Image or Anima. Type a seed for repeatable results, or connect a **Random Integer** node to the seed for a new one on every run. * **Images and latents.** Models work on compressed *latents*, not pixels. **Image to Latents** encodes an image with a VAE, for image-to-image; **Latents to Image** decodes the result back into pixels. * **Scaling.** **Scale Image** and **Resize Image** resize pixels, **Scale Latents** and **Resize Latents** resize latents, and **Image-to-Image** runs an upscaling model. Latents are already compressed, so enlarging the image and then refining it often gives more detail than enlarging the latents. * **Control and LoRAs.** A **ControlNet** node turns a control image, usually prepared by a processing node such as **Canny Edge Detection** or **Depth Anything Depth Estimation**, into a control input for the denoise node. **Apply LoRA** nodes (one per model family, such as **Apply LoRA - SDXL**) add a LoRA to the model’s UNet and text encoders. * **Iteration and batches.** **Iterate** runs the rest of the graph once for each item in a collection, and **Collect** gathers several values into a collection. For example, **Random Range** makes a list of seeds and **Iterate** feeds them one at a time to the noise node, generating one image per seed. For more complex repetition, see [Loop Nodes](/users-guide/workflows/loop-nodes/). ## Adding community nodes [Section titled “Adding community nodes”](#adding-community-nodes) The community has written many more nodes, from image effects to prompt tools. The easiest way to install a node pack is the [Custom Node Manager](/users-guide/workflows/custom-node-manager/): paste the pack’s Git URL and it is downloaded and loaded without restarting. To install one by hand, clone or download it into the `nodes` folder of your InvokeAI root, then click **Reload** in the Custom Node Manager or restart InvokeAI. `git clone` is the better choice, because `git pull` then updates the pack. The [Community Nodes](/users-guide/workflows/community-nodes/) page lists available packs. ## Keyboard shortcuts [Section titled “Keyboard shortcuts”](#keyboard-shortcuts) These work while the workflow editor has focus. On macOS, use **Cmd** in place of **Ctrl**. | Shortcut | Action | | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | **Shift+A** or **Space** | Add a node | | **Ctrl+C** / **Ctrl+V** | Copy / paste nodes, with the connections between them | | **Ctrl+D** | Duplicate the selected nodes | | **Ctrl+A** | Select all nodes | | **Delete** / **Backspace** | Delete the selected nodes | | **Ctrl+Z** / **Ctrl+Shift+Z**, **Ctrl+Y** | Undo / redo | | **Shift**-drag | Box-select nodes | | Hold **Ctrl** while dragging | Snap to the grid | | **Ctrl+Enter** | Invoke |

# Face Tools Nodes

The Face Tools nodes detect faces with MediaPipe and provide utilities for identifying, masking, and extracting faces in workflows. The current nodes are in the `segmentation` category and use version `1.2.2`. ## FaceIdentifier [Section titled “FaceIdentifier”](#faceidentifier) **FaceIdentifier** outputs a copy of the input image with detected face IDs printed on each face. Use it first when you need to target a specific face with FaceMask or FaceOff. Face IDs are numbered from `0`. Detection order can change if the image changes, so run FaceIdentifier again after editing an image. ### Inputs [Section titled “Inputs”](#inputs) | Input | Description | | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Image | Image to face detect. | | Minimum Confidence | Minimum confidence for face detection. Lower this if detection is failing. | | Chunk | Bypass full-image face detection and use chunking. Chunking is also used automatically if no faces are found in the full image. | ### Outputs [Section titled “Outputs”](#outputs) | Output | Description | | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- | | Image | The input image with face ID numbers drawn on detected faces. | | Width | Output image width in pixels. | | Height | Output image height in pixels. | ## FaceMask [Section titled “FaceMask”](#facemask) **FaceMask** creates a mask for detected faces on the input image. Leave **Face IDs** empty to mask all detected faces, or provide a comma-separated list such as `0,2,7` to target specific faces. Use FaceIdentifier to find the IDs. The mask can be adjusted with X and Y offsets if detection is slightly too large or small. Enable **Invert Mask** to affect everything except the detected faces. ### Inputs [Section titled “Inputs”](#inputs-1) | Input | Description | | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Image | Image to face detect. | | Face IDs | Comma-separated list of face IDs to mask. Leave empty to mask all detected faces. | | Minimum Confidence | Minimum confidence for face detection. Lower this if detection is failing. | | X Offset | Offset for the X-axis of the face mask. | | Y Offset | Offset for the Y-axis of the face mask. | | Chunk | Bypass full-image face detection and use chunking. Chunking is also used automatically if no faces are found in the full image. | | Invert Mask | Toggle to invert the mask. | ### Outputs [Section titled “Outputs”](#outputs-1) | Output | Description | | ------ | -------------------------------------- | | Image | The original image, converted to RGBA. | | Width | Output image width in pixels. | | Height | Output image height in pixels. | | Mask | The generated face mask. | ## FaceOff [Section titled “FaceOff”](#faceoff) **FaceOff** extracts a single detected face into a bounded image and returns a matching mask plus paste coordinates. Use FaceIdentifier to find the face ID before targeting a specific face. Padding expands the bounding box around the detected face. This gives downstream processing more context and increases the bounded image size while keeping the face in place within the crop. ### Inputs [Section titled “Inputs”](#inputs-2) | Input | Description | | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Image | Image for face detection. | | Face ID | The face ID to process, numbered from `0`. Multiple faces are not supported. | | Minimum Confidence | Minimum confidence for face detection. Lower this if detection is failing. | | X Offset | X-axis offset of the mask. | | Y Offset | Y-axis offset of the mask. | | Padding | All-axis padding around the mask in pixels. | | Chunk | Bypass full-image face detection and use chunking. Chunking is also used automatically if no faces are found in the full image. | ### Outputs [Section titled “Outputs”](#outputs-2) | Output | Description | | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Image | The bounded face image. If no face is found, the original image passes through. | | Width | Output image width in pixels. | | Height | Output image height in pixels. | | Mask | Mask matching the bounded image. | | X | X coordinate of the bounding box’s left side. | | Y | Y coordinate of the bounding box’s top side. | ## Tips [Section titled “Tips”](#tips) * Use the same **Minimum Confidence** value in FaceIdentifier and the FaceMask or FaceOff node that consumes the IDs. * Enable **Chunk** if not all target faces are detected. Full-image detection and chunked detection can produce different results. * Lower **Minimum Confidence** when detection fails, but watch for false positives. * Adjust X and Y offsets if the mask is too large, too small, or shifted. * Add FaceOff padding when the extracted face needs more surrounding context. * Face detection can fail on heavy face paint, hair covering the face, extreme angles, or other obstructions.

# Automating with Workflows

> Why and when to use workflows, how nodes and connections work, a tour of the workflow editor, and a walkthrough that generates a subject with SDXL, composites it onto a background, and builds a simple form for it.

The Generate panel, the Canvas and the Video panel each cover a common job well. **Workflows** are for everything else. A workflow is a recipe of processing steps that you assemble yourself: generate an image, then upscale it, cut out its subject, place it on a background, run it through a second model, repeat it for a list of prompts, and so on. Once built, a workflow runs with one press of **Invoke** and can be reused, adjusted and shared. Use a workflow when you want to: * **Chain steps together** that would otherwise take several trips through different panels, such as generating an image and then compositing it onto another. * **Use features the panels do not expose**, including community-contributed nodes. * **Repeat a process** exactly, on new prompts or images, without redoing it by hand. * **Share a process** with others as a single file. ## Nodes and connections [Section titled “Nodes and connections”](#nodes-and-connections) A workflow is made of **nodes** connected into a graph. Each node performs one operation, such as loading a model, encoding a prompt, denoising, decoding an image, or resizing it. Everything InvokeAI does is built from nodes, including what the Generate panel does behind the scenes. A node has: * **Outputs**, listed at the top of the node, with connection points on its right edge. * **Inputs**, listed below the outputs, with connection points on its left edge. Most inputs also have a control for entering a value directly, such as a text box, number or model picker. You build a workflow by dragging from an output of one node to an input of another. The connection passes the output’s value along, and the input’s own control is replaced by *Provided by connection*. Connection points and lines are colored by the kind of value they carry, such as images, latents, conditioning, numbers or text, and only compatible points can be connected. An input marked with a red **\*** is required: the workflow cannot run until it has a value or a connection. When you press **Invoke**, InvokeAI works out the order to run the nodes from their connections, runs them, and saves the images from the nodes you chose to the Gallery. ## A tour of the workflow editor [Section titled “A tour of the workflow editor”](#a-tour-of-the-workflow-editor) Workflows are built and run in the **Automate** layout (**Alt+4**). The editor fills the center, the workflow’s form is on the left, and the Gallery and Queue are on the right. Hover over a numbered circle, or tap it on a touchscreen, for a short description. | | Part | What it does | | -- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | **Workflow panel** | The workflow’s **form**: its most important settings as simple controls, like a Generate panel for this workflow. | | 2 | **View** / **Edit** | **View** uses the form. **Edit** lets you design the form, edit the workflow’s details (name, description, author, tags, notes), and inspect the selected node. | | 3 | **Editor toolbar** | Tools for panning, box and lasso selection, and erasing nodes or connections; **Zoom in**, **Zoom out** and **Fit view**; **Download workflow as PNG**; and **Node opacity**. | | 4 | **Workflow name** | The active workflow. Click it to open the **Workflows** library. | | 5 | **Workflow actions** | **Add node** (**+**), **Save to library…**, the save status, settings, and the **⋯** menu with **Workflow details…**, **Rename workflow…**, **Import workflow JSON…**, **Export workflow JSON**, **New workflow** and more. | | 6 | **The graph** | The workflow’s nodes and connections. Drag nodes by their title bar; scroll to zoom; drag empty space to pan. | | 7 | **Minimap** | An overview of the whole graph for finding your way around large workflows. | | 8 | **Gallery and Queue** | Where results appear, with the Queue, Preview and Image Map on the right-hand rail. | | 9 | **Automate** | The layout preset for workflows. | | 10 | **Invoke** | Runs the active workflow. The routing control beside it shows the source (**Workflow**) and the destination (**Gallery**). | ### The essentials [Section titled “The essentials”](#the-essentials) * **Add a node** by pressing **Shift+A** or **Space** in the editor, or with the **+** button in its header, then search for it by name. * **Connect nodes** by dragging from an output on the right of one node to an input on the left of another. * **Choose which images are kept.** Only nodes with **Save to Gallery** checked, at the bottom of image nodes, send their images to the Gallery. * **Manage workflows** from the **Workflows** library: click the workflow’s name in the editor’s header. The [Workflow Editor Reference](/users-guide/workflows/editor-reference/) covers all of this in detail, along with connectors, the library, common node patterns, community nodes and keyboard shortcuts. ## Walkthrough: put a generated subject on a background [Section titled “Walkthrough: put a generated subject on a background”](#walkthrough-put-a-generated-subject-on-a-background) The Generate panel can make a picture of a fox, but it cannot then cut the fox out and place it on a photo of your choice. This walkthrough builds a workflow that does both: it generates a subject with SDXL on a plain white background, then uses the **Image Compositor** node to remove the white and composite the subject onto a background image. Finally, it gives the workflow a simple form. You need an SDXL model and an SDXL VAE, such as the *sdxl-vae-fp16-fix* starter model, installed from the Model Manager, and a background image in the Gallery. ### 1. Start from the SDXL text-to-image workflow [Section titled “1. Start from the SDXL text-to-image workflow”](#1-start-from-the-sdxl-text-to-image-workflow) 1. Press **Alt+4** for the Automate layout. 2. Click the workflow’s name at the top of the editor to open the **Workflows** library, go to **Browse**, and open **Text to Image - SDXL**. A copy is added to your project and becomes the active workflow. 3. In the **Main Model - SDXL** node, choose your SDXL model in **Model**, and in the **VAE Model** node choose an SDXL VAE. 4. In the **Positive Prompt** node, describe the subject on a plain background, for example *a red fox sitting, full body, on a plain white background*. A plain, evenly lit background is what lets the Compositor cut the subject out cleanly. This workflow already contains the SDXL text-to-image chain: the model loader, positive and negative prompts, random seed and noise, **Denoise - SD1.5, SDXL**, and **Latents to Image - SD1.5, SDXL**, which turns the result into an image. ### 2. Add the Image Compositor [Section titled “2. Add the Image Compositor”](#2-add-the-image-compositor) 1. Press **Space** and type *compositor*, then click **Image Compositor** to add it. Drag it to the right of **Latents to Image**. 2. Connect the **Image** output of **Latents to Image** to the **Image Subject** input of **Image Compositor**. 3. In **Image Background**, click **Choose image** and pick a background from the Gallery, drag one onto it from the Gallery, or **Upload** a file. 4. Check **Save to Gallery** at the bottom of **Image Compositor**, so the finished composite is saved. Uncheck it on **Latents to Image**, unless you also want to keep the plain subject. ![The Latents to Image node connected to the Image Compositor node, which has a mountain landscape as its Image Background. Save to Gallery is unchecked on Latents to Image and checked on Image Compositor.](/_astro/workflow-compositor-nodes.Cd4aiUfe_Z1bYjdm.webp) ### 3. Run it [Section titled “3. Run it”](#3-run-it) Press **Invoke**. The nodes light up in turn as they run, and the composited image appears in the Gallery. Press Invoke again for a new variation: the workflow’s **Random Seed** node picks a new seed each time. The default settings rarely give a clean cut-out on the first try. SDXL models usually add a soft shadow under the subject, even with *shadow* in the negative prompt. The Compositor’s default flood fill, which spreads inward from the corners of the subject image, stops where the white turns to the shadow’s light grey, so the shadow and sometimes a pale halo are pasted onto the background. To clean them up, set **Chroma Key** to `white` and raise **Threshold** to about 80, as in the example below, and run it again. Every near-white pixel then becomes transparent, including the faint shadow. Watch the light parts of the subject A chroma key also removes near-white areas *inside* the subject, such as a fox’s white chest or the highlights in its eyes. If holes appear, lower **Threshold** until they close, accepting a little shadow, or describe a subject without white parts. ![After a run: the Latents to Image node's latest output shows the fox on a plain white background, and the Current Image node shows the fox composited onto the mountain landscape. The Image Compositor uses Chroma Key white and Threshold 80.](/_astro/workflow-compositor-result.CGHfP7vg_1UAdNu.webp) In summary, the **Image Compositor**’s settings are: * **Threshold** (default 50) sets how different from the background color a pixel must be to count as part of the subject. Raise it if a white halo or shadow remains around the subject; lower it if parts of the subject disappear. * **Chroma Key** removes a specific color everywhere instead of flood-filling from the corners. Enter a color such as `white` or `#00ff00`. This also removes faint shadows and background showing through gaps in the subject. Leave it empty to use the flood fill. * **Fill Y** (on by default) scales the subject to the height of the background; **Fill X** scales it to the width. Keep at least one of them on unless the two images are exactly the same size. With both on, the subject is stretched to the background’s shape. * **X Offset** and **Y Offset** move the subject, in pixels. Positive values move it right and **up**. A subject moved past an edge reappears on the opposite side. ### 4. Build a form for the workflow [Section titled “4. Build a form for the workflow”](#4-build-a-form-for-the-workflow) A workflow with a dozen nodes is not the most convenient thing to use day to day. The **form** in the Workflow panel on the left gathers the settings you actually change into one simple panel, like the Generate panel. To add a setting to the form, click the **pin** icon at the right end of its row in the node (**Add to form**). Only settings with their own control can be pinned; connected inputs cannot. 1. The SDXL workflow already puts its **Positive Prompt**, **Negative Prompt**, **Model**, VAE and board settings in the form. 2. In **Image Compositor**, pin **Image Background**, **Threshold**, **X Offset** and **Y Offset**. The pins turn blue, and the settings appear at the end of the form. 3. In the Workflow panel, click **Edit**, then **Form**. Each setting is a card: * Drag a card’s title bar to reorder it. * Type in **Field label** to give it a clearer name, such as *Background* for Image Background. * Click **✕** (**Remove from form**) to take out settings you do not need, such as the VAE and board. * **Add form element** adds a **Heading**, **Text**, a **Divider**, or a row or column container to group settings. 4. Click **View** to use the form. ![The Workflow panel in Edit mode, with the Form tab listing the pinned settings as cards and the Node Inspector below.](/_astro/workflow-form-edit.eiuveVOy_22Rfoa.webp) In **View**, the form works like any generation panel: change the prompt or the background and press **Invoke**. The form is part of the workflow, so it is saved with it, exported with it, and shown to anyone who opens your workflow. ![The finished form in View mode: Positive Prompt, Negative Prompt, Model, the Image Background with a mountain landscape, Threshold, X Offset and Y Offset.](/_astro/workflow-form-view.BuhN2McG_hSfJR.webp) ### 5. Save and share it [Section titled “5. Save and share it”](#5-save-and-share-it) Use **Details** in the Workflow panel’s Edit mode to give the workflow a name and description, then click **Save to library…** in the editor’s header to keep it in your library for other projects. To share it, choose **Export workflow JSON** from the **⋯** menu. ## Learn more [Section titled “Learn more”](#learn-more) * [Workflow Editor Reference](/users-guide/workflows/editor-reference/) — nodes, connections, the library, common node patterns and shortcuts in detail. * [Loop Nodes](/users-guide/workflows/loop-nodes/) — repeat steps over lists of prompts, images or values. * [Face Tools Nodes](/users-guide/workflows/face-tools/) — find, mask and edit faces in a workflow. * [Community Nodes](/users-guide/workflows/community-nodes/) and the [Custom Node Manager](/users-guide/workflows/custom-node-manager/) — add nodes written by the community. * [Migrating from ComfyUI](/users-guide/workflows/comfyui-migration/) — how familiar ComfyUI nodes map to InvokeAI’s.

# Loop Nodes

> Repeat workflow steps over a collection and optionally carry values from one iteration to the next.

Loop nodes let a workflow repeat the same group of steps for every item in a collection. For example, a workflow can process every image found by a detector, try several seeds, or build a collection of results one item at a time. The main loop uses two nodes: * **For** starts the loop and provides one collection item at a time. * **ForReturn** marks the end of the loop body and sends the result back to the loop. ## The Basic Pattern [Section titled “The Basic Pattern”](#the-basic-pattern) Connect the nodes in this order: 
```text
Collection producer -> For.collection
For.loop_linkage - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - > ForReturn.loop_linkage
For.item -> work nodes -> ForReturn.output
For.output_collection -> nodes after the loop
```
 The `For` node has one iteration for each item in its `collection`. During an iteration, its `item`, `index`, `total`, and `state` outputs contain values for that iteration. The work nodes run, then `ForReturn` closes that iteration. The `For` node does not send its per-item `item` output directly to nodes after the loop. To run a node once after all iterations finish, connect that node to `For.output_collection` or `For.final_state`. You can connect `For.output_collection` directly to a branch input on an `If`. If that branch is selected, its consumer runs in the parent frame after the loop finishes; you do not need a `For.final_state` edge just to make it run. The editor draws a dashed green boundary around the loop body. This is a visual guide showing which nodes repeat; the boundary does not carry data. The dashed green line between `For.loop_linkage` and `ForReturn.loop_linkage` is a required association, not a data value. The remaining values move through the ports and edges you connect. The loop is not executable until its two boundary nodes are paired. Connect `For.loop_linkage` directly to the matching `ForReturn.loop_linkage`. When you add `ForReturn` from an iteration-output connection in the node picker, the editor can create this association for you. Replacing either boundary node requires pairing the replacement again. Deleting a connector preserves its through-connections by reconnecting the upstream source to surviving downstream targets. Deleting a complete loop-linkage alias collapses it to a direct `loop_linkage` edge; ordinary connector paths remain ordinary data edges. ### A Simple Example [Section titled “A Simple Example”](#a-simple-example) To process every image in a collection: 
```text
Image collection -> For.collection
For.item -> Image Processor.image
Image Processor.image -> ForReturn.output
For.output_collection -> Save or display node
```
 The processor runs once per image. The final `output_collection` contains the processed images in the same order as the input collection. `ForReturn.output` may be disconnected when the result is carried through loop state instead. A body still needs a dependency into `ForReturn`, such as a state update or a scalar `continue_condition`; there is no separate completion port for effects-only bodies. ## What The For Outputs Mean [Section titled “What The For Outputs Mean”](#what-the-for-outputs-mean) | Output | Meaning | Use it for | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | | `loop_linkage` | The association port for the matching `ForReturn` | Pairing the loop boundaries; it is not data | | `item` | The current collection item | The work done during this iteration | | `index` | The zero-based position of the current item | Labels, counters, or position-based logic | | `total` | The collection length | Progress or position-based logic | | `state` | The current loop state | Values carried from earlier iterations | | `output_collection` | All values returned through `ForReturn.output` | Work that should happen after the loop | | `final_state` | The state from the last completed iteration | Reading accumulated values after the loop | The `item`, `index`, `total`, and `state` outputs belong inside the loop body. The `output_collection` and `final_state` outputs become available after the loop finishes. `loop_linkage` is only for pairing the two boundary nodes. Collection Cartesian products are limited to 100,000 item pairs. A product larger than 100,000 pairs fails with an error instead of expanding without bound. ## Returning Results [Section titled “Returning Results”](#returning-results) `ForReturn` closes the loop body. It has four useful inputs: * **Output** adds one value to `For.output_collection` for the current iteration. Null (`None`) values are retained, so collection positions continue to match iteration order. * **State** supplies the state for the next iteration. * **Continue Condition** controls whether another item should be processed. It continues by default; connecting `False` stops after the current iteration. * **Loop Linkage** pairs this node with its owning `For`. It must be connected directly to `For.loop_linkage`; it does not provide a value to the loop body. The `Loop Linkage` connection is separate from the body data connections. It tells the engine which `ForReturn` closes which `For`, which matters when loops are nested or several loop boundaries are present in one workflow. ## Carrying Values With State [Section titled “Carrying Values With State”](#carrying-values-with-state) State is an optional set of named values that travels from one iteration to the next. It is useful for a running sum, a changing parameter, or several values that must be updated together. The state helper nodes make this easier: * **Empty Loop State** creates a blank state. * **Get Loop State Value** reads a value by name. Its `default` input is used when that name has not been set yet. * **Set Loop State Value** returns a copy of the state with one named value changed. * **Merge Loop State Values** returns a copy with several named values changed. A running value usually looks like this: 
```text
For.state -> Get Loop State Value.state
For.item -> Add or other calculation
Get.value + For.item -> calculation
calculation -> Set Loop State Value.value
Set Loop State Value.state -> ForReturn.state
For.final_state -> Get Loop State Value.state (after the loop)
```
 Set the `default` on `Get Loop State Value` when the value does not exist during the first iteration. For example, use `0` for the initial value of a running sum. State is separate from `output_collection`: * Use `output` when each iteration produces a result that should be collected automatically. * Use state when the loop needs to remember or update a value while it runs. * Use both when the loop needs per-item results and an accumulator. ## Making Collections For A Loop [Section titled “Making Collections For A Loop”](#making-collections-for-a-loop) `For` accepts one collection input. Use collection-producing nodes before it when the values need to be calculated. ### Range Nodes [Section titled “Range Nodes”](#range-nodes) * **Integer Range** creates values from `start` up to, but not including, `stop`. * **Integer Range of Size** creates a requested number of values. * **Random Range** creates a collection of random integers using its seed and bounds. For example: 
```text
Integer Range of Size -> For.collection
For.item -> work nodes
```
 This is useful when the loop should run a known number of times. The integer itself can be used as a seed, index, or ordinary numeric input. ### Combining Collections [Section titled “Combining Collections”](#combining-collections) These nodes make the collection relationship explicit before the loop: * **Concatenate Collections** puts every item from the first collection before every item from the second. The two collections may have different lengths. * **Zip Collections** pairs items by position. Both collections must have the same length; a mismatch is an error. * **Cartesian Product of Collections** creates every possible pair, one item from each collection. The collections may have different lengths. Products larger than 100,000 pairs fail with an error. Choose based on the relationship between the items: 
```text
Concatenate: first phase, then second phase
Zip:         first[0] with second[0], first[1] with second[1], ...
Cartesian:   every item in first with every item in second
```
 An empty input to `Concatenate` is harmless. An empty input to `Zip` is valid when both inputs are empty. An empty input to `Cartesian Product` produces no pairs. ## For And Iterate [Section titled “For And Iterate”](#for-and-iterate) Both `For` and `Iterate` repeat work over a collection, but they serve different purposes: * Use **Iterate** when a normal workflow needs to expand a collection into separate executions and **Collect** when those executions should be gathered again. * Use **For** when the repeated work has a clear beginning and end, needs loop state, may stop early, or should expose a final collection and final state. An `Iterate` can also be used inside a `For` for a bounded inner pass. The inner values must be gathered by one `Collect` before the outer `ForReturn`: 
```text
For.item -> preparation -> Iterate.collection
Iterate.item -> inner work -> Collect.item
Collect.collection -> ForReturn.output
```
 The outer loop waits for the inner `Iterate` and `Collect` to finish, then returns one collection for that outer item. One exact serial two-`Iterate` body is also supported: `For.item` feeds a preparation node and the first `Iterate`; its item feeds a second preparation node and `Iterate`, followed by one work node, one `Collect`, and `ForReturn`. For this bounded pattern, use a non-empty literal outer collection and one consumer of `For.output_collection`. Other arrangements, such as sibling internal `Iterate` nodes or an independent external `Iterate` feeding a `For` body, are unsupported. ## Nested For Loops [Section titled “Nested For Loops”](#nested-for-loops) A `For` can contain another `For`. The inner loop must finish before the outer loop returns its current item: 
```text
OuterFor.item -> InnerFor.collection
InnerFor.item -> inner work -> InnerForReturn.output
InnerFor.output_collection -> OuterForReturn.output
```
 Each `For` must have its own matching `ForReturn`. The editor and saved workflow keep those pairings separate, so state from an inner loop does not automatically become state for the outer loop. Connect values explicitly when they need to cross a loop boundary. Multiple inner loops can be used as siblings when their final collections feed an ordinary collection-combining node. That node defines whether those collections are concatenated, zipped, or combined as a Cartesian product. The workflow does not choose one of those meanings automatically. ## Empty Collections And Early Stop [Section titled “Empty Collections And Early Stop”](#empty-collections-and-early-stop) An empty collection is a successful loop with zero body iterations: * `output_collection` is empty. * `final_state` is the provided initial state, or an empty state. * No body node runs. Set `ForReturn.continue_condition` to `False` when the loop should stop after the current item. The results and state from completed iterations remain available through the normal final outputs. ## Collection Type Checks [Section titled “Collection Type Checks”](#collection-type-checks) Before a workflow runs, InvokeAI checks the item types flowing through `Collect`, `Iterate`, and connected `If` nodes. An `int` and a `float` collected together have the common item type `float`, so an iterator consumer must accept a float. If both resolved branches of an `If` feed one `Collect.collection`, their possible item types must share one compatible root. For example, `If(Collect[int], StringCollection) -> Collect.collection` is rejected even though only one branch runs at a time; the resulting collection cannot have one statically known item type. Complete both `If` branches before relying on strict type validation or queueing the workflow. A workflow saved before stricter collection checks may now fail validation when queued. Follow the validation error to the collector or iterator connection, then update the workflow so its collection item types and consumers agree. ## Common Wiring Mistakes [Section titled “Common Wiring Mistakes”](#common-wiring-mistakes) * Connect the collection to `For.collection`, not to `For.item`. * Connect `For.loop_linkage` directly to the matching `ForReturn.loop_linkage`. * Connect body work to `ForReturn.output` when its results should be collected. * Connect after-loop work to `For.output_collection` or `For.final_state`, not to `For.item` or `For.state`. * Give each nested `For` its own `ForReturn`. * Use `Zip Collections` only when the input lengths must match. * Use `Cartesian Product of Collections` carefully: large inputs can produce many pairs. For the execution and validation rules behind these connections, see the contributor reference: [`Loop Nodes Architecture`](/contributing/loop-nodes/).
